1 **Translator’s Note**
*This is an English translation of Tecnologías Espirituais: Reza, Roça e Sustentabilidade entre os Kaiowá e Guarani, by Anastácio Peralta,* originally published in Portuguese by Pedro & João Editores (São Carlos, 2025). It was produced with the assistance of an AI language model (Claude, Anthropic) at a reader’s request, and is not an official or publisher-authorized translation.
Passages originally recorded in the Guarani language — including direct oral testimony from community members — have been left untranslated and appear here exactly as in the original, since machine translation of Guarani is unreliable. Portuguese-language text, including the surrounding narration and framing of those testimonies, has been translated into English. Bibliographic references are left in their original language and form, following standard academic citation practice. Pagination differs from the Portuguese original because English text does not occupy the same space as Portuguese; the table of contents below reflects this English edition’s own pagination.

**About the Author**
*Kwarahy Rendyju, Ava Yvy Poty: radiant sun, flower of the earth*
I am Anastácio Peralta, son of Conceição Medina and dona Bonifácia Peralta, born in Dourados, Mato Grosso do Sul, in the village of Te'ýikue, municipality of Caarapó, on May 2, 1960. Currently 61 years old, I am single, a teacher, a Kaiowá farmer, a student, a researcher, a master's graduate, a doctoral candidate, and a witness to the social changes that have taken place among my people since the times when we lived free in our territory. Along this trajectory I became an observer of confinement to reservations, of expulsion to the back lots of ranches and cities, of the search for traditional territories, of the violence suffered at the hands of governments, and of the violence suffered from the anti-indigenous population of the State.
Over the course of my sixty-one years of life, as the son of this couple who spent little time with me, since my father passed away while I was still in early childhood, I grew up in the village of Caarapó and on the ranches in the surrounding area. I started school past the age of eight, but I learned little because I was afraid and did not understand what the teachers said, and besides, from a very young age I already had to go to work, so school at that time was something quite distant from my reality.
In this social context I did not remain in school. I helped care for the settlers' children, tend animals, and plant and harvest in my family's fields. I entered a stable relationship while still young and became father to Devanildo Ramires Peralta. To support my family, I worked handling cattle on a ranch, and later went to work in cattle drives, crossing the state from north to south, from west to east, through rain, cold, or scorching sun.
11
On the cattle drive I was cook and companion to the other members. But I dreamed about the children who walked alongside the rural schools we passed by. I dreamed of one day becoming a teacher, an educator. Time went by, and in the 1990s I went to live in the village of Dourados. I worked as a bagger at the company Cotrijui, and during this period I had the joy of finding, and being found by, the Missionary Indigenous Council (CIMI), where I formed a beautiful friendship with Hilário Paulos, who encouraged me in this dream of becoming an educator.
I studied through the Brazilian Literacy Movement (Mobral) and through Youth and Adult Education (EJA), where I had the opportunity to contribute by assisting in meetings and reflections on the difficult moment faced by the Jaguapiru and Bororó reservations, in the municipality of Dourados, in the face of a strong wave of suicides, which I called the death industry caused by the colonialist system.
I was also, for many years, quite involved in organizing the Aty Guasu movements (the Great Assembly of the Guarani and Kaiowá Peoples), and after many conversations and reflections with the male and female prayer leaders, I began turning my senses toward seeking to understand why we lived and suffered discrimination. It was at that moment that I stopped accepting and began questioning everything that involved me and involved my people. So, at this point in my life, I began to turn toward my people, to observe, feel, and contemplate our whole life and our existence. I reflected that even after so much theft, so much genocide, so much violence, we remain alive, resisting and existing, and, most of the time, with joy and hope.
With this idea in mind and in my heart, in 1994 I began the project “Teko Joja,” in the village of Dourados, whose objective was to delve into theories and practices of good living for our
12
indigenous people, cultivating ideas about fields, crops, and sustainability through Kaiowá and Guarani eyes. This journey of learning and reflection alongside my people led me, in 1999, to join the Ara Verá project - a Normal-level Secondary Course for the Training of Guarani and Kaiowá Teachers, after taking placement exams to
test out of primary school (elementary education). This project was born from the struggle of the Kaiowá and Guarani, from the demands that existed at that moment.
It was in this phase of my life that I found another love, with whom I built a relationship and had a beautiful daughter, Camila Snarde Peralta, daughter of Braulina Snarde, a great companion in the struggle for school education, for the women's movement, and for our territories, which the government still does not recognize despite the studies. However, life goes on its course, and we separated. In 2001 I took part in the Coordination of Indigenous Affairs, in the Popular Government of the Municipality of Dourados, and in 2008 I became a member of the National Commission on Indigenist Policy - CNPI, of the Ministry of Justice.
Thus, during this time of walking the path, of studies supported by the male and female missionaries of CIMI, together with the brothers and sisters, companions of the Workers' Party (PT), whom I believe to be allies in the indigenous cause, I had the opportunity to be an active member of the working group that helped shape the city of Dourados under the government of then-mayor Laerte Tetila, of the Workers' Party (PT). In that administration I worked in the Secretariat of Government, was an advisor to the training group of the Ará Verá Project through the State Secretariat of Education, was an employee of FUNAI, worked in the sector of Agriculture and Local Development; and also had the opportunity to contribute as advisor and consultant
13
to the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), of the United Nations (UN).
In 2008, I entered the Indigenous Intercultural Faculty (FAIND), an achievement won through much struggle by all the Kaiowá and Guarani, together with so many friends who continue the fight for FAIND to truly be the space where our knowledge receives its due value and is not usurped by the karaí, since the non-indigenous logic is to turn it into merchandise.
I graduated with great difficulty, being part of the movement and having, on countless occasions, to leave classes and go to the struggle in
local, national, and international mobilizations. This delayed things somewhat, but I completed my degree with great care, in the Human Sciences track of the Teko Arandu Indigenous Intercultural Teaching Degree program.
With great joy I had the opportunity to contribute, on this journey of mine, as a speaker at various state and municipal elementary and secondary schools and at universities throughout Brazil, and even at the European Parliament, where, besides learning and teaching, I used the space to denounce the injustices we live through. I have taken part in several audiovisual documentaries, such as: “Sementes de sonhos” (2009), “À sombra de um delírio verde” (2010), and Yvy Poty – Flores da Terra (2018).
I also took part in various training courses, such as: political and social training, solidarity economy, permaculture courses, experiential learning, and project management; with the aim of exchanging knowledge about our spirituality, fish farming, horticulture, and the management of Agroforestry Systems (SAFs), among many others that were quite important for
14
building connections among allies.
I ran as a candidate for federal deputy in 2014 for Mato Grosso do Sul (MS), for the PT, and was not elected. I received 2,622 votes (0.21%) in the coalition “Mato Grosso do Sul com a força de todos” (PT, PR, PDT, PROS, PTC, PCdoB, PTB, PSDC). A few months after the election, I left the party because I disagreed with the thinking of the majority members of the Party in Dourados and in the state of Mato Grosso do Sul.
Today I live in the Tekoha Panambizinho, where I was adopted by my people as an heir-son of the struggle and the reconquest of this land. I have been here since 2010, where I have sought to understand the local cosmovision. Together with the community, I have sought partnerships and alliances so that we might jointly think through and carry out projects of self-sustainability and territorial self-management.
In this way, in this tekoha, I have supported the school, at times as an educator, at times as an education volunteer, in addition to working on building a space of free education, which is
referred to by the community as the Free University of Indigenous Peoples and for Indigenous Peoples. We seek alliances with people who fight in defense of Mother Earth and who believe in the pedagogy of nature, so that this place may be built by many hands, so that the university may be able to function freely, without dependence on the State's education systems. May it be from indigenous to indigenous, and intercultural, in the exchange of knowledge among peoples who fight for and defend the diversity of life.
In 2019 I entered the master's program, after receiving encouragement from friends and refusing to accept the way the surrounding society treats me and treats my people. I thus
15
decided to research and study more, so that I could better understand what this perverse system thinks of and has in store for me and for all the descendants of my people; because, being prepared, I can engage in dialogue on equal terms, and I can better defend my people's way of being and living, which is not static and which has been harmed ever since the colonizers invaded our territories. This thesis was defended in the master's program in Education and Territoriality at the Federal University of Grande Dourados-UFGD, under the supervision of professor Dr. Laura Jane Gisloti. These reflections are now published in book form by the Graduate Program in Geography at UFGD, where I am currently pursuing my doctorate.
I wrote this work in the midst of the Covid-19 pandemic, a product of this perverse and selfish system, which has caused the death of many people, and this saddens me greatly. Thus, becoming a master's graduate at a historical moment of such relevance is a way of seeking the means to make myself visible in a society that does not see us, that exploits us, and that rejects our history, our language, and our right to have our sacred places, the territories of Ñanderu Guasu and its flowers.
I am Kwarahy Rendyju, Ava Yvy Poty, I am radiant sun, flower of the earth, born to admire and contemplate the beauties of the Creator, and with great joy and satisfaction, I invite you, readers, to walk together with me and feel my emotions and sensations.
16
**Presentation**
This book records and seeks to understand the spiritual technologies used by the Kaiowá and Guarani, which I define as the negotiations carried out between human and non-human beings in rituals and ceremonies performed for the planting, harvesting, and consumption of certain foods cultivated by the Kaiowá and Guarani peoples.
**The Tekoha Where I Live, Dwell, and Exist: Panambizinho Indigenous Land**
The Panambizinho Indigenous Land (TI), at the time of colonization, was distributed among the immigrants who came from various parts of the country. However, my kinspeople, who were being taken to the Dourados and Douradina reservations, resisted the system, causing discomfort at the time to the governments and to the new “owners” of the land. The State, believing that at some point the indigenous people would integrate into the surrounding non-indigenous society, decided that the Aquino, Concianza, and Pedro family groups would remain in the Panambizinho region, occupying 60 hectares of land.
Thus, these families found themselves hemmed in among the karaí, working as laborers clearing land and in the fields, but they always maintained their spirit of belonging, praying for more than 60 years, according to stories heard during home *visits. Dona Odalicia, now passed on, told me that: “My father and I and everyone who lived here, we prayed hard to Ñanderu1, to the Hexakáry2, to get our tekoha back”. This story is still repeated today* by elder men and women and children connected to these family lineages.
17
1 Our father. 2 Spiritual leader, seer
After so many prayers, anthropological studies, and struggle against the governments, in 2004, under the government of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, official recognition was won for the area called Yvy Akãndiré, corresponding to 1,272 hectares, which, according to what the elders tell, is part of the great Tekoha Guasu3. It was the spiritual struggle that secured the reconquest of this territory for them. However, they received this land deforested into pastures, with a few structures such as tanks, a pig shed, and some dwellings, but with almost no natural wealth remaining. The forest that had once been present in the region no longer existed.
During this period, amid the development of policy for indigenous school education, in keeping with this community's aspirations, the municipality's first indigenous school emerged, which came to be called the Pai Chiquito - Chiquito Pedro Indigenous School, in the Panambizinho Indigenous Land. Also emerging, through Ara Verá4 students Arnaldo and Misael, were many questions regarding the territory, its customs, its culture, its spirituality. Thus, these two residents of Panambizinho were the first indigenous people to begin writing the history of this territory, since before, it was only the karaí who wrote it.
And so, observing the wounded, sorrowful, bare land that would not offer them conditions for a long life, these two researchers from Panambizinho sought partnerships and also pursued the implementation of the public policies offered by governments and partner organizations (See appendix 1).
All of these projects brought people together in their design and execution; however, much as they answered a wish of the population, many mistakes occurred in their development, since most of the indigenous people did not take ownership of the techniques offered and did not use the goods made and/or
18
produced. As a result, the investments made were substantial in quantity, but very little bore fruit.
3 Greater Kaiowá and Guarani territory. 4 Normal Course at Secondary Level for the Training of Guarani and Kaiowá Teachers.
Today the community has nearly 90% of its land under monoculture production, such as soybeans and corn, all transgenic, grown under an agreement made between the landowners and the Terena people of the Dourados village, to whom they pass on, per harvest, amounts equivalent to the production. According to Mrs. Fineida Aquino Concianza, "it's what we have to give our children! Better conditions for food, clothing, among other things" (Fineida; Panambizinho).
Thus, after we recovered the land, which we received with joy, with much singing and dancing, we realized that it came to us sick. It was entirely degraded, its plant cover made up only of colonião and brachiaria grasses. This is one of the reasons I hold responsible for leading many Panambizinho families to abandon the system of communal cultivated fields, because for many years they lived in a space that did not offer adequate conditions for the Kaiowá to reproduce their traditional way of being and living.
The degradation of our land was brought about by the ignorant way in which the karaí (non-indigenous people) managed the land, first through the excavation of the soil for large-scale ceramic production, such as roof tiles and bricks. Afterward came cattle ranching and the monoculture of soybeans and corn, which caused the land to be trampled and poisoned. The soil is now so compacted that subsoiling5 has become necessary for the land to become fit for planting once again.
19
This situation means that many families, even today, continue to depend on the federal government's basic food baskets, which have been provided to this village since 1995. It is a very complicated situation, since the food offered is not as healthy as our traditional diet, given that the foods making up the basic food basket are always industrialized and ultra-processed. Often, these foods cause illness among
5 This is a technique used to loosen the soil layers so as to reduce compaction, promote tillage, and thus facilitate rooting, water penetration, and soil aeration.
my people, such as high cholesterol and diabetes, illnesses that are highly prevalent in the villages of Dourados.
Panambizinho is also served by the CRAS (Reference Center for Social Assistance), with weekly appointments, and by medical care twice a week provided by a multidisciplinary team.
Today Panambizinho, the little butterfly, flies high in search of new air to live...
**Tape porã: the beautiful walk of research thought, felt, and built on the ground of the territory**
This research was a continuation of my undergraduate thesis carried out in the Teko Arandu Indigenous Intercultural Teacher Training Program, at the Faculdade Intercultural Indígena, with the aim of continuing the reflections on sustainability, good living, seeds, land, and spiritual technology among the Guarani and Kaiowá.
To guide the methodological procedure, I drew on the work of indigenous scholars who had lived through analogous situations in their own research contexts, as was the case with Izaque João (2011), João Paulo Barreto (2013), Tonico Benites (2014), Eliel Benites (2014,
20
2020), Gileandro Barbosa Pedro (2020), Sônia Pavão (2021), Marcilene Lescano (2021), among other works produced by indigenous researchers.
At the outset, I did readings aimed at guiding the conduct of the fieldwork, focusing on indigenous authors, with the intent of disciplining the eye and the ear, in order to make the most of the ethnographic record and of the dialogue with the participants who generously contributed to the construction of this research.

* Odarícia Concianza (in memoriam).
  As I am a researcher indigenous, researching my own life setting, a series of resources were mobilized that gave me access to routine situations, experienced in the day-to- day life of the community, which facilitated my reflections and dialogues. In this sense, the fieldwork was structured in two movements, where in the first, observation was carried out on a participant basis, taking part in and recording the rituals, ceremonies, baptism celebrations, and the planting and harvesting of foods, such as white corn, in the greater Dourados region, covering the
  ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
  21
  villages of Panambizinho, Panambi, and the Laranjeira Nhanderu land reclamation. Then, in the second moment, I drew on the wisdom and spiritual understanding of the spiritual and political leaders of my people, and so I selected the following interviewees, who are the intellectuals who hold all of the ancestrally systematized indigenous knowledge: Dona Odarícia, as she is known through her history, appears as Alice Pedro on her identity document, the RG. Wife of Lauro Concianza. Ñandesy prayer leader. She was born on August 20, 1920 and passed away on December 6, 2015, at the age of 95, in the Tekoha Panambizinho, municipality of Dourados. She raised her children through great struggle, on the 60 hectares of land, leaving much of her knowledge recorded in various books and publications about this tekoha. She gave us an immense legacy of teachings and examples. She is deeply missed!
* Nailton Aquino, 78 years old.
  Second son of Paulito Aquino, singer of ghahu and kotyhu. Born on April 5, 1944, in Kaiowá territory, he lived his youth working on farms in the region, started a family, was widowed with his children still young, remarried, this time to his current
  22
  wife, Mrs. Noêmia, with whom he had two children. He lives in Panambizinho, municipality of Dourados.
* Nelson Concianza, 90 years old.
  Eldest son of Lauro Concianza and Odarícia Pedro. Married to Rosalina Aquino. Keeper of the crosses, prayer leader Ñanderu. He was born in the village of Panambi, on May 3, 1932. His life was guided by work alongside his community, he worked on farms in the region, married Mrs. Rosalina and had several sons and daughters. He suffers from the aftereffects of a stroke, but continues to teach his descendants the importance of the crosses, the prayers, and the songs. He lives today with his family in Panambizinho, municipality of Dourados.
* Jairo Barbosa, 84 years old
  23
  Son-in-law of Paulito Aquino. Native of Panambi Lagoa Rica. Ñanderu prayer leader and currently responsible for the Jerosy Puku. He was born in Saverá, in the Tey'ikwe indigenous reservation, municipality of Caarapó. He worked for many years on farms, passing through several states of the federation, including alongside the Maxacali people, in Minas Gerais, a place he dreams of returning to. He started a family, was widowed with young children, and raised them, teaching them his knowledge, and after some years decided to marry again. He went to live in Laranjeira Ñanderu, separated, and today lives in Panambi Lagoa Rica, municipality of Douradina, where he started a new family.
* Valdomiro Oswaldo, 64 years old
  24
  Born in a time of the dispossession of his people, son of João Aquino and Marcelina Costa da Silva, grandson of Paulito Aquino. He was raised by his grandparents, as was the custom of the time. Married to the Ñandesy prayer leader Roseli Concianza Jorge, with whom he built a family, with prayers and songs as their heritage.
* Jorge Gomes, 62 years old
  ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
  25
  He was born on January 5, 1959. He lives in the village of Pirakua, in the municipality of Bela Vista, where through prayers and much struggle they reclaimed their traditional territory. He is a Ñanderu prayer leader, political leader of his community, and actively participates in the struggles for the guarantee of the original and constitutional rights of his people. He was coordinator of the Aty Guasu and is currently an active advisor.
* Valério Vera Gonçalves, (in memoriam), 73 years old
  Ñanderu prayer leader and advisor. He was born on February 19, 1948, in Jataivera Lima Campo, from where he was expelled along with his people, but through the struggle they reclaimed part of the territory, which was recognized and returned to the relatives. He provided assistance to the tekoha, such as Kokwe’i, in Xiru Karai. He was very active in his mission of praying for people, but, as every flower must be picked, he went to adorn the heavenly gardens on March 20, 2021. He was living in Panambi Lagoa Rica Village, in the municipality of Douradina.
  26
* Eliel Benites, 42 years old
  Professor and Director of the Indigenous Intercultural Faculty (FAIND/UFGD). He was born and lives in the Tey’ikue village, municipality of Caarapó. He holds a degree in Intercultural Teaching Degree for Indigenous Peoples, Teko Arandu, and a master’s degree in Education from the University Dom Bosco Catholic University (UCDB), and a Ph.D. in Geography from UFGD. He is part of the Movement of Guarani and Kaiowá Teachers and is an active member of the Cultural Association of Indigenous Filmmakers (ASCURI).
* Marilda Duarte, 53 years old
  27
  Ñandesy prayer leader. Artisan. Specialist in traditional medicine and Guarani craftwork. She lives in the Bororó Indigenous Reserve of Dourados.
  And finally, Fineida Aquino Concianza, 47 years old, daughter of Nelson Concianza and Rosalina Aquino, born in Panambizinho, municipality of Dourados. It was not possible to record an image of Fineida.
  Drawing on the dialogues, reflections, and observations shared with these people who helped me build this research, I sought to understand how Kaiowá and Guarani agricultural theory is configured, taking into account the relationship with human beings, non-human beings, the surrounding world, and food production. The ethnographic record, from an indigenous perspective, makes it possible to place this material in dialogue with the formulations produced by indigenous researchers from other peoples and other traditional communities, as well as by non-indigenous researchers.
  28
  I sought to investigate and ethnograph the food-production rituals among the Kaiowá and Guarani, with special attention to the spiritual technologies used in the making and management of Kaiowá and Guarani gardens (roças). I call Spiritual Technologies the negotiations carried out between human and non-human beings in the rituals and ceremonies performed for the planting, harvesting, and consumption of certain foods cultivated by the Kaiowá and Guarani. This is our Kaiowá and Guarani science.
  In this sense, I deepen the reflection on Indigenous Science with the thinking of the Kaiowá anthropologist Celuniel Valiente, which reflects the shift in the academic paradigm of which this work is part. We, Indigenous Peoples, once regarded merely as interlocutors of research, have come to occupy the role of indigenous researchers and protagonists of our own epistemological systems, proposing a respectful and just dialogue between the sciences:
  Indigenous science cannot be characterized as lesser than Western science, but rather thought of through the interaction or dialogue between these different forms of knowledge that exist in the world. It is also necessary to remove indigenous knowledge from the traditional conception, that is, to discard it from the sphere of antiquity in which it is perceived as old and outdated; through a deeper look at this
  knowledge, one perceives the epistemological value it holds (VALIENTE, 2018, p. 202).
  ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
  29
  30
  **Preface**
  We are faced with a precious text, a true challenge to our modern, technological, and productivist culture. This is a study by a Kaiowá-Guarani indigenous author, Anastácio Peralta, *entitled: “Spiritual Technologies: Prayer, Cultivated Fields, and Sustainability among the Kaiowá and Guarani”.*
  To understand his vision we must adopt another paradigm, one very close to the contemporary paradigms of deep ecology, quantum physics, and modern biology. The whole text is a dialogical confrontation with the modern way of relating to nature and with the mechanized production of the goods that sustain our life and culture.
  The author, a professor and researcher, speaks in the first person. Methodologically, he first immerses himself in the indigenous reality of several villages (tekoha), observing the rhythm of life and the work, especially the rituals and festivals. He then consults, in long conversations, the guardians of ancestral culture, the elder women and men, retrieving ancestral wisdom and memory. Third, he interviews specific indigenous men and women, always providing a brief biography of the interviewees, as well as of the elders. From this he systematizes the accumulated knowledge, always in dialogue with our dominant culture.
  Peralta represents well the cosmology of most native peoples. He puts it aptly: “The worldview of indigenous peoples rejects the separation between the human and nature, which greatly distinguishes it from the Western worldview. For us indigenous people, we are not separate from nature, we are part of it, or, better still, we are nature itself. This philosophy leads us to approach the world around us with care and respect, for if we
  31
  harm nature we harm ourselves.”
  He gives clear meaning to his writing: “In this dissertation, I, Anastácio Peralta, of the Kaiowá people, who since childhood have fought for survival, bring in my own history and in the history of my people the desire for us to be protagonists and sovereign, as we once were in the past, with regard to food, territorial, and spiritual sovereignty.”
  For the Kaiowá-Guarani, everything is suffused with life; everything forms one great community of life that encompasses all human beings, the mountains, the waters, the plants, the animals, and especially the seeds. All life demands respect, veneration, and the cultivation of the sacred dimension. Different is the “karai reko,” the way of life of white people and moderns. For them, the earth and nature, with everything that exists within them, have a merely utilitarian function, a reality without purpose in itself, available for human exploitation.
  The central axes of the theoretical framework revolve around the themes of territory (the so-called reserves, always under threat), the seeds, white corn, and the “tekoha” (the village). But the driving axis of it all consists in spiritual technology. It is made up of sacred rituals, long prayers, and interaction with visible and invisible life (energies-spirits).
  Peralta shows — and herein lies the singularity of his research — that we do not need the machines of the modern paradigm to produce everything we need. Moreover, the very use of such apparatuses, however sophisticated, offends Mother Earth.
  There is another way of producing and also of healing that uses the spiritual energies present in all beings — these are the spiritual technologies. He says: “I call Spiritual Technologies the negotiations carried out between human and non-human beings
  32
  in the rituals and ceremonies performed for the planting, harvesting, and consumption of certain foods cultivated by the Kaiowá and Guarani. This is our Kaiowá and Guarani science.”
  The clearest example of this spiritual technology is revealed in the seeds: “they possess a complex
  spiritual technology, capable of dying and reviving, bearing fruit and feeding the other living species of planet Earth.” The seed, with reverence, is placed in the lap of Mother Earth and is cared for at every one of its stages. It represents the perpetuity of life and of human nourishment.
  Moreover, Peralta deepens the central question of spiritual sustainability, in the sense of creating all the conditions for the Kaiowá and Guarani life-system and existence to remain alive and healthy. Indigenous peoples have created the category equivalent to the Andean “bien vivir,” which they call “teko porã.”
  This vital energy present in all things is evoked through prayer. Prayer, guided by the prayer leaders (ñanderu and ñandesy), is fundamental because through it they enter into communion with the essence of life that manifests in all beings, but reaches its greatest concentration in the seeds. They state with conviction: “We, Kaiowá and Guarani, believe that as long as we remain steadfast in the pursuit of techniques arising from the spiritual world, we hold the hope of full life within us, indigenous peoples, and within all the other beings who inhabit this world.”
  Peralta approaches the theme critically with regard to transculturality. He realizes that the relationship between Kaiowá-Guarani culture and our own is asymmetrical. However hard white people try to approach indigenous people in a friendly way, it is always a look from above to below. There is an
  33
  immense disproportion between the dominating force of modern culture, grounded in power-domination over nature, and indigenous culture, founded on the nature of which they feel themselves bearers. They are nature, and they love and care for it. And white people devastate it to the point of endangering all life. We white people seek, at most, an alternative development, whereas they seek an alternative to development. They present it through spiritual technologies.
  Peralta realizes how modern culture penetrates especially the young. They belong to two worlds, the modern and
  at the same time, they take part in the life and ritual festivals. But he notes a spiritual weakening.
  I want to stress the importance of the fact that the Kaiowá themselves are training their own researchers with their own outlook, better than those who come from outside with a different outlook. We have much to learn from them, for our civilization seems to have reached its own limits. The researcher and professor Peralta gives us a fine example of this innovative research.
  Let this confession by Peralta serve as our conclusion: “It is precisely against this spiritual weakening that we fight, it is for this continuity of life that we resist. We, the Kaiowá and Guarani Kwery, are concerned not only with our human life, but we are also concerned with the natural balance, we are concerned with spiritual lives; the seeds give us examples of resistance when they react to every attack and thus, unrestrained and exuberant, make use of their spiritual techniques and teach us generosity.”
  If one day our civilization should collapse for having destroyed the foundations that sustain all life — and this is not impossible, since we have created the very principle of self-destruction — it will be through the worldview and the
  34
  values so well represented by Kaiowá-Guarani culture that the survivors will be able to refound a friendly and caring way of inhabiting our Common Home. Through this research, Anastácio Peralta hands us the undying seed of a future of hope and of the joy of living.
  *Leonardo Boff*
  35
  **The Kaiowá and Guarani Peoples: forest peoples, peoples of struggle!**
  The great Guarani People speak languages belonging to the Tupi-Guarani linguistic trunk and are organized into three peoples: Guarani Mbya, Guarani Ñandeva, and Guarani Kaiowá. This book focuses on the Guarani Kaiowá and Guarani Ñandeva peoples, the second-largest indigenous group in Brazil, who live in the state of Mato Grosso do Sul, where they call themselves Kaiowá and Guarani, or Guarani and Kaiowá. I am part of this Great People!
  The strip of territory traditionally occupied by the Kaiowá and Guarani, in the southern cone of the state of Mato Grosso do Sul, was quite extensive and lay between the Apa River and the Serra de Maracaju. This territory came to occupy a considerable stretch from east to west of the Serra de Amambai, encompassing much of the Brazil-Paraguay border (Pereira, 2007).
  Today these peoples find their territories greatly diminished, such that they now occupy small areas located in a strip of land on each side of the Brazil-Paraguay border region, where they are called Pãi Tavyterã (MELIÀ, 1976).
  The occupation of territories by these peoples has always been linked to areas rich in natural resources considered suitable for maintaining the Kaiowá and Guarani way of being, that is, the teko. In this sense, they established their villages, or tekoha, in areas close to rivers and forests. Beyond this, the selected area had to be free of disease and of threats from malignant spirits (PEREIRA, 2016).
  By origin and tradition, we Kaiowá and Guarani are forest farmers; we practice hunting and fishing and gather seeds, fruits, and other natural riches offered by Mother Earth in our territory.
  36
  However, our territory today finds itself
  extremely reduced and damaged owing to the ignorance of the karaí (non-indigenous people), who see nature as a commodity and take from it everything possible, without thinking of the consequences.
  Recent surveys estimate the Kaiowá and Guarani population at more than 50,000 individuals (PEREIRA, 2016). Our relatives are living in eight reserves and fourteen indigenous lands, totaling 22 indigenous areas. However, since the late 1990s, the number of areas occupied by the Kaiowá and Guarani has been gradually growing. This is because our people have been reorganizing and are thus claiming and demanding the demarcation of our traditional lands expropriated by agribusiness occupation. This movement is characterized as the reclaiming of the ancestral territory that was stolen, and it draws on the strength of the traditional masters, the Ñanderu and the Ñandesy (BENITES, 2014).
  Nowadays, most of the Kaiowá and Guarani live in indigenous reserves, which were created in the early twentieth century (between 1915 and 1928) by the Indian Protection Service (SPI) (CAVALCANTE, 2014; PEREIRA & MOTA, 2012). The function of these reserves was to shelter the indigenous people who were being expelled from their ancestral territories, which were plundered and impoverished by colonization projects that had captured the minds of the karai with the idea of development.
  The ignorance and racism of white people are made explicit in the process of occupying agricultural areas in Mato Grosso do Sul. It is a policy stemming from an idea that disregards the rights of native peoples and treats us as though we were not people worthy of rights. This brutal way of conducting policy
  37
  has brought disastrous consequences to the environment and to our culture, brutally impacting the native vegetation and promoting great imbalances in the local ecosystems of the Kaiowá and Guarani, in addition to destabilizing our way of living, understanding the world, and walking our path.
  Amid all this complexity in which my people live, I describe and analyze the knowledge, practices, and rituals mobilized by the Kaiowá and Guarani peoples, especially the spiritual technologies involved in the production of gardens (roças) and food. More specifically, I focused on understanding the knowledge mobilized for the rituals, ceremonies, and festivals practiced by the Kaiowá and Guarani, past and present, in the tekoha and reserves, for the planting and harvesting of food.
  To that end, I present how Kaiowá and Guarani agricultural theory is configured, so as to understand the forms of care given to seeds and plantings, and the planting-tool technologies used in the past and in the present day. Beyond this, I seek to understand how the spiritual technologies used for Kaiowá and Guarani sustainability are organized.
  **Kaiowá Sustainability: indigenous science in defense of Mother Earth**
  We, Guarani and Kaiowá, have a specific worldview, defined as our particular way of seeing, thinking, ordering, and feeling the world. In this way of seeing and feeling the world, there is a strong relationship between the Kaiowá and Guarani worldview and culture, with visible and invisible beings, with spirituality, and with the celestial planes.
  Thus, indigenous worldviews must be considered within the context of their cultural values and environmental knowledge. In this way, each indigenous people has its own worldview, which
  38
  in turn relates to the specific context in which each people is situated, such that territorial and ecological aspects influence their vision of the world.
  The worldview of indigenous peoples rejects the separation between the human and nature, which greatly distinguishes it from the Western worldview. For us indigenous people, we are not separate from nature, we are part of it, or, better still, we are nature itself.
  This philosophy leads us to approach the world around us with care and respect, for if we harm nature we harm ourselves.
  For non-indigenous people, nature is at the service of human beings, which is why they exploit its riches endlessly. For us indigenous people, the human being is nature; we are interconnected within a single web of life, each caring for the other. Nature, for us, is a living being, one that must be admired, cared for, and loved. And just as we do not separate humans from nature, we do not separate nature from culture, as non-indigenous people do.
  In this way, the Kaiowá and Guarani worldview, driven by a spiritual mindset of care and respect for Mother Earth, prevents the development of an economy based on the notion of exploitation and profit, as occurs in the capitalist system. In the Kaiowá and Guarani socioeconomic system, of a cooperative type, work is carried out through a feeling of solidarity rather than of competition.
  The concept of sustainability is a concept from the non-indigenous Western world and is related to the term “sustainable development.” These concepts reflect the perspective of that which seeks to meet the needs of the current generation without compromising the life and needs of future generations. In this sense, the logic of these concepts aligns with
  39
  the idea of producing profits, being socially just, and environmentally sound (SACHS, 2002).
  Thus, for the researcher Rosa Colman, another aspect that cannot be dissociated from local development and territory is the question of sustainability. “Addressing sustainability and local development presupposes living under a new ethic, guided by commitment and responsibility toward the promotion and defense of life in all its senses” (COLMAN, 2009).
  One of the intellectuals of the quilombola people, Antônio Bispo dos Santos, known as Nêgo Bispo, offers a highly important reflection on aspects of sustainability. This quilombola and traditional master
  reflects on the obstacles between the thinking and the practice of sustainability as carried out at the hands of the colonizers:
  In contemporary debates we can also perceive some efforts at transfluence, when we analyze the attempts to combine different principles and/or perspectives within some productive processes such as: sustainable development, production organic, agroecological, agroforestry, permaculture, ethnodevelop- ment, etc. It is an attempt to bring together thoughts, concepts, and values. However, when we move on to actually imple- menting these thoughts, concepts, and values, we once again encounter major confrontations (SANTOS, 2015, p. 51).
  With regard to indigenous sustainability, the anthropologist Dominique Tilkin Gallois reflects:
  “Sustainability” is considered a goal, an objective, not a public policy. If any sustainability policy exists, it can only be an indigenous policy. Formulating a public policy of “indigenous sustainability” would necessarily lead us into serious contradictions. In the indigenist field, public policies are currently aimed at meeting emergency demands, practicing a form of assistentialism that has already shown itself to be, and continues to be, the main cause of the rupture in the sustainability of the indigenous way of life. For this reason, this text prefers to speak of
  40
  sustainability as a goal, just as indigenous autonomy is also considered a goal. This text proposes that there should be a more detailed discussion of how, in projects supposedly aimed at indigenous sustainability, the entire system of production, distribution, and consumption is worked out, taking into account the importance and the value that indigenous groups attribute to the logic of exchange, of giving and receiving. Everything indicates that, in many cases, the “culture of projects” has encouraged the transformation of this logic into a much simpler equation: receiving support through projects with no precise goal other than the drafting of the next project (GALLOIS, 2005, p. 1).
  Thus, it becomes necessary to develop internal and external policies to guarantee the sustainability of our people, with regard to our spirituality, our territories, our food, and the environment with all its diversity of fauna, flora, and beings. In this sense, I am not referring only to sustainability as it is conceived in the world of the karaí, where they think only of profit and of land as personal, commercial property, where wealth is extracted from Mother Earth without regard for her death and the consequent death of all living beings.
  Also on the subject of Kaiowá and Guarani sustainability, the Kaiowá author and researcher Sônia Pavão, from the Limão Verde village, reflects:
  That the search for balance in our Mother Earth needs to be thought of as a collective, community action to strengthen and restore the richness of nature. This means that, for us, the plants, the animals, the water, the earth, the air, the stones, the mountains — in other words, everything that makes up the planet has life and deserves to be cared for and protected. Un- like white people, who see everything as merchandise and think only about making money off the death of nature (PAVÃO, 2021, p. 121).
  Building on this notion of territory and sustainability, for the Kaiowá and Guarani it is not possible to achieve sustainability merely by recovering small parcels of land, as the testimony of the Kaiowá researcher Eliel Benites demonstrates:
  41
  We are living through a moment of reconstruction: a new direction after the disaster of confinement; we perceive the urgency of the land question, our reserves are small and degraded. Policies are needed that know how to handle all the differences, even from village to village, without continuing with isolated actions. Policies of community reorganization through technical training of the community and based on the community's own vision. The community's unity has been broken down; the community itself lacks clarity about what it wants. Enabling communities to rethink their own lives. This organization has to be strong in order to engage
  with the surrounding community. Preparation aimed at strengthening indigenous knowledge. Not transplanting indigenous knowledge into the white system, but building the system of indigenous knowledge. Only in *this way is sustainability built (URQUISA, 2006:2 apud BENITES, 2014).*
  Reflecting on the need to move beyond the Western concept of sustainability in order to truly glimpse and understand the notions on this theme that involve the cosmology of indigenous communities, the researcher Rosa Colman notes:
  To approach the concept of sustainability from the standpoint of indigenous communities, it is essential to understand the concept of nature. And to do this it is necessary to disarm oneself of the orthodox, Western, and capitalist concept, which perceives nature in a hierarchical way, as domination, and in a separate, compartmentalized way. And to observe with sensitivity and realize that it is possible, as it is for indigenous peoples, to relate to nature in a different way, without “dominating,” without so much “transforming,” and more by understanding the different processes that occur there. Thus, sustainability for these populations depends more on the capacity for understanding, respect, and integration than on the domination and transformation of nature (COLMAN, p. 92).
  I came to understand that the term sustainability, for my people, means working collectively, admiring, caring for, and loving our Mother Earth, because we need worlds that are sustainable. Mother Earth asks for our help. But for us, Kaiowá and Guarani, it is not possible to have sustainability without having the land, without having our territory, which was stolen and destroyed by colonizing hands. We need the land because
  42
  she is the one who gives us life, who nurses us. And it is the land that also gives us the strength to produce food, to produce life.
  But it is not only the land that guarantees our Kaiowá and Guarani sustainability. We also have spiritual sustainability, in which prayers, songs, rituals, and celebrations are
  very important and must always be practiced. We have to pray, we have to sing in order to produce food, for the rain to come, to baptize the land, to plant the seed, and for the harvest. So sustainability is a whole, a system, that is part of our indigenous science, our Kaiowá and Guarani science.
  So, according to our science, it is not only food that will guarantee our sustainability. For us, Kaiowá and Guarani, being sustainable is something broad and complex, in which it is necessary to build a healthy environment, starting from where we live, from where we dwell. The water has to be healthy, and so do the plants, from those that are food to those that are medicine and those that are firewood.
  To produce all this sustainability, we need good-quality land, a healthy, living land, full of joy, able to shelter many beings and plants, but to achieve this harmony we also need a great deal of spiritual management, of care, of rain. And we indigenous people, Kaiowá and Guarani, also understand the importance and value of spiritual sustainability, because spirituality is what gives us the strength to keep our prayers, our songs, and all our ritual firm — the ritual that makes the earth nourish itself, the seed germinate, the rain fall, and the plants grow.
  The land, the soil, is the cradle of the seed; it is where the seed remains dormant, sleeping until the rainwater falls, descending from the sky to bless the seed. Then, the moment the water falls, the seed awakens and begins to take root and to
  43
  sprout. In this view, sustainability is a set of forces, of movements, of events, which need to happen in a dynamic and synchronized way. Everything has to be interconnected, has to happen at the right time, in the right moon for planting, with the right amount of rain, on the right day. And the harvest, too, has to be carried out at the exact moment, the sacred moment, to celebrate and give thanks so that, next year, it will come back for us to plant and have food again.
  A sustainable people must be strong in its faith, and this spirituality involves many aspects that govern the life of my
  people. For this reason, I approach Kaiowá and Guarani sustainability through the following subthemes: spiritual sustainability, territorial sustainability, food sustainability, and environmental sustainability, since, according to our Kaiowá system, these concepts are part of a holistic vision, one that looks not only at the materialized aspect of the world and of society, but, in a deeply humanized way, observes the interior of beings and their inner health — that is, it is concerned with practicing living well.
  Here it is important to note that the separation of the aspects of Kaiowá and Guarani sustainability into subthemes was done for the sake of organizing the text, but it is important to stress that these four aspects are intimately related to one another and are interdependent and complementary.
  **Spiritual Sustainability**
  44
  Figure 1. Meeting with the Ñandesy of Panambizinho. Source: Xiru Karaí Archive.
  After listening to elders, both men and women, I set myself to understanding what the karaí understand by sustainability in spiritual matters, and I was then surprised by some of the meanings and statements of
  non-indigenous thinkers who are also concerned with planetary life. Among my inquiries, what struck me most and gave me the greatest grounding was an interview in which the philosopher Leonardo Boff explains that the transition to a sustainable society includes reducing consumption, reusing and recycling materials, and changing the economic system. The philosopher stressed that all of this only gains consistency if it is supported by a spirituality, in the sense of understanding that everything is connected to the whole. Thus, it becomes clear that it is important to live this dimension not only in awareness, but as a lived experience. He adds that sustainability means guaranteeing that all beings have available to them the conditions to live, reproduce, and remain alive in their
  45
  ecosystems (BOFF, 2014).
  In this way, sustainability is a systemic concept whose principal aspect, for us Kaiowá and Guarani, is spiritual maintenance and strengthening. This is the thinking of my people and of so many other peoples who live in harmony with life in all its magnitude.
  And on this journey of mine, perceiving the cultural and consequently spiritual weakening of my people, while at the same time observing the perseverance of my brothers and sisters in the struggle for the tekoha, I felt a restlessness in my being, searching for what would be necessary for us to become self-sufficient once again. Thus, I sought to understand what sustainability is for the Kaiowá Guarani, through the elders, the Ñanderu and Ñandesy; and with this knowledge I felt encouraged to contribute to the elders who struggle through prayer, who seek in Ñanderu Guasu words of wisdom, of consolation, of hope, of accomplishment.
  Reflecting on the last few decades, I sense the estrangement and the flood of other religions entering our territories, causing uncertainties and doubts among the younger generations; that is why I wanted to understand the reason for the spiritual weakening of my people, which is one of the tragic consequences of the loss of our territory.
  On this point, I turned to historical reflection, going back to colonial Brazil, and I was able to see that, in every era, there was present in the minds of the
  colonizers the idea that we were a people without faith. Yet the faith of the peoples of the Americas was never monotheistic, as it was among the other peoples of the West. So I reflected that in our culture there is no single God; rather, there are many spirits, the owners of each created being.
  46
  On these differences between the conception of colonizing Western spirituality and that of the Original Peoples, the quilombola intellectual and master Nêgo Bispo prompts us to reflect on religiosity as a preponderant factor in the process of colonization, noting:
  Believing that religion is a privileged dimension for understanding the diverse ways of living, feeling, and thinking about life among different peoples and societies, it is important to understand the differences and the dialogue between the monotheistic worldview of the colonizers and the polytheistic worldview of the counter-colonizers, reflecting on their effects and consequences in the processes of colonization and counter-colonization (SANTOS, 2015, p. 12).
  In this way, our spiritual sustainability is upheld by the Ñanderu and Ñandesy, who keep the songs, prayers, and basic teachings for everyday life, as set out by the Kaiowá researcher Eliel Benites during this research: “living the ava reko means respecting the rules of one's people, such as living out the rituals with respect, with the teachings, performing the prayers, always living with a smile” (Eliel Benites, Tey'ikue).
  On these same foundations that sustain the Kaiowá Guarani way of being, in the pursuit of living well, Nanderu Valério reflects:
  We have to live smiling and happy. For this there is the prayer that every day I have to do in order to live. To have the ava reko we need the teko porã, which is based on harmony among families, on having food of our own, a specific care that is ours. But today our families are disorganized, family leaders are weakened. I feel that they are all guaxos because they are not heard, and seek to resolve their problems by seeking out the so-called political leadership (captain), who also does not resolve them. Nowadays, I see that parents and grandparents have lost the power of
  speech, and so we are living the ava karaí, without space, without fauna and flora. This way it is impossible to teach the traditional way of being, and an example of this is that people no longer grow roça crops, because there is a basic food basket available, and so there is no longer a need to
  47
  plant. In this way the prayer leaders, the elders, lose their values and respect. This has happened since the arrival of the non-indigenous way of being. The churches do not like indigenous people to go hunting, fishing. If they see indigenous people practicing these activities, they expel them right away.... In this sense, if the ava reko is vai, pochi, the tekoha is bad, and because of this, we need to seek ways to revive the communities so they carry out their rituals, such as kunumy pepy (the passage from the child cycle to adulthood, where boys learn songs, prayers, and how to behave like true Kaiowá) and, thus, rekindle the flame of spirituality and of Kaiowá culture (Valério Vera Gonçalves, Panambi Lagoa Rica).
  Building on the reflection of Ñanderu Valério and of our brother, the quilombola community leader Nêgo Bispo, especially in his work Colonização, Quilombos: modos e significações (SANTOS, 2015), it is possible to draw a parallel, addressing and reflecting on how the State and the Church have committed, and still commit to this day, the crime of erasing, silencing, and killing spirituality against our ancient cultures: these institutions have worked, since colonialism, to put an end to our spiritual sustainability.
  However, we indigenous peoples know how to develop a truly peaceful connection with nature, and for that we know that we must first learn to develop a respectful and non-violent relationship with ourselves. This transformation requires important inner work. When this work is combined with greater awareness and understanding of the subtle changes we wish to bring about in ourselves, we begin to appreciate our true spiritual personality and to live according to that knowledge. It is at this moment that we find our spiritual sustainability.
  We know that the seed of spiritual sustainability lies in thought and action. If it lies in thought and action, then how do we use this energy so that we may always live in
  aragwyje, that is, in fullness with the spiritual and material beings? Along these lines, the great companion, educator, and
  48
  researcher Veronice Lovato Rossato, in her master's thesis, cites Paulito Aquino, a respected Kaiowá cacique who warns: "Only with prayer can we calm violence, only with song can we cool people's tempers" (ROSSATO, 2002, p. 44).
  The author confirms Kaiowá thought when she says that the word (nẽ'ẽ ayvu) is the center and origin of everything; it is the germ of life, the "divine substance" of Ñanderu (Our Father), from which people proceed. When a child begins to speak, it means that the spirit has manifested within them, that is, life in its fullness, our essence, our true being. The word is voice, speech, language, tongue, soul, name, life, origin, personality (ROSSATO, 2002, p. 31). Therefore, to strip us of the right to speech is to deny our teko, our existence, and thus to undermine our spiritual sustainability.
  When I lived with Paulito, Balbina, and their family, I learned that Ñanderu created all languages as different from one another. I was also taught that language is our very soul, and without it we are nothing; without it we are unrecognizable before God. That is why, when we stop speaking our language, we lose our soul, our spirituality, and we can no longer maintain dialogue with Ñanderu. We are left lost in the cosmos, not knowing where or when to act. For us, the Kaiowá and Guarani peoples, there is no nẽ'ẽ without teko, no teko without nẽ'ẽ, and no tekoha without ava. That is, there is no life without soul-word and vice versa, just as there is no territory without its original inhabitants and their jara (divine owners).
  In this way, it is essential that each people ensure the use of their language wherever they may be, so that we may maintain our spirituality, regardless of our acquiring other languages to dialogue with other human beings. To speak with Ñanderu, one must live the rituals and speak our mother tongue, for He comprehends and understands all the languages He created.
  49
  Keeping our language strong also strengthens spiritual sustainability.
  But colonization nearly destroyed our system when, through the Pombaline law, it stripped us of the right to communicate in our own language. When the government created the SPI (Indian Protection Service), it placed so-called captains at the head of the peoples, who, entangled with the church—that is, "converted" to evangelicalism or Christianity—demonized and even physically assaulted the prayer leaders, carrying forward the project to destroy the strong language and spirituality of the Kaiowá Guarani.
  On the path of resistance to this process of violation, the sensibility of spirituality through traditional prayers gives rise to a collective connection, of intuition and affectivity, manifesting the true and manifold Kaiowá and Guarani way of being, as the indigenous researcher Elemir Martins reflects (2020). In his own words: "The words of the prayers are sacred, inspired by the Guarani words of the mediator between the earthly world and the supernatural world" (MARTINS, 2020, p. 52).
  Ñembo'e (prayers) and porahei (songs) guide existence, orient traditional knowledge and territorial self-management, and also lead to sustainability, besides constituting the seed that germinates resistance for life, for territory, and for autonomy. It is in this sense that I stress the importance of spirituality in the territorial struggle as a fundamental axis in the construction of sustainable life in the Kaiowá and Guarani view. In the words of Kaiowá and Guarani researcher Elemir Martins:
  The Ñanderu gained prestige in the struggle against oppression, for being guardians of knowledge, which is why they are regarded by many indigenous people as the principal religious leaders. (...) The generation of prayer leaders who are in the struggle today went through a period of preparation, during which they actively took part in every religious activity
  50
  of the old indigenous spiritual leaders, for these knew what was to come. In this sense, they invested in the preparation of future prayer leaders. The Kaiowá and Guarani cosmology, according to the prayer leaders, is strengthened by the power of prayer and indigenous wisdom (MARTINS, 2020, p. 87).
  From this perspective, nurturing spiritual sustainability is the most fundamental and important step so that the entire sustainable system of Kaiowá and Guarani life and existence can remain alive and healthy. It is from spiritual sustainability that the other sustainabilities derive. It is the fundamental axis that allows us to live in a harmonious and healthy world. And even in the face of so many violent attacks, the Kaiowá and Guarani peoples remain steadfast in the struggle to maintain all indigenous spirituality, which is fundamental to enabling the existence of our people.
  **Territorial Sustainability**
  Figure 2: Meeting with the Ñandesy and the Ñanderu in Panambizinho. Source: Xiru Karaí Archive.
  According to our system, the famous phrase of the late Bartomeu Melià (in his memory), "without tekoha there is no teko," defines our system well: the existence of the territory is essential for there to be a healthy environment and sustainable
  51
  food; but all of this is only viable if it is sustained by the technology of spirituality.
  According to Kaiowá researcher Eliel Benites, the category of traditional territory and the origin of the Kaiowá and Guarani are
  present in the narratives of prayer leaders (Ñanderu and Ñandesy) and make possible a better understanding of the great wisdoms of these peoples "in relation to their territoriality or the place where they live, and also the cultural and sacred elements that contribute to defining the importance of the cosmological meanings of the land, according to traditional culture" (BENITES, 2014, p. 35).
  Kaiowá historian Gileandro Barbosa Pedro stresses the need to maintain the connection with the territory and its guardians, so that occupation strategies "are guided by the way of life arising from the ava reko, which, in turn, should be lived in harmony with the well-being of the teko (traditional way of living)" (PEDRO, 2020, p. 31). To build the tekoha, the place had to be suitable and undergo the process of prayer to drive away evil spirits, thus confirming the interconnection between spirituality and territoriality for our people.
  In the past, we Kaiowá and Guarani had an environment that was sustainable by nature. It was a complete body lacking nothing; we ourselves and nature served one another mutually, in harmony. But the system of the karaí, that is, colonialism and capitalism, sold the idea that quality of life and social ascent necessarily pass through consumption, as Boff points out (2009).
  Thus, in order for some to consume to the fullest, others must consume insufficiently. "It is inhuman and irrational that 327 families possess nearly half of all the wealth on Earth, and that three individuals have more income than 48 countries where
  52
  600 million people live. This represents an offense against human rights," the philosopher stresses (BOFF, 2009, p. 1).
  The fact that he is a convinced humanist does not, however, prevent Boff from being critical of the mechanistic view of nature that became consolidated in the twentieth century. The philosopher believes that we must overcome anthropocentrism and the illusion that the human being is the center of everything. According to Boff, the human being is a link in the chain of life, for
  life is one and unitary. In this way, all living beings are made up of the same 20 amino acids and the same four phosphate bases. Therefore, we are all brothers and sisters (BOFF, 2009, p. 1).
  On the developmentalist policy of recolonization by the State, which in Kaiowá and Guarani territory unconditionally supports agribusiness and completely destroys any attempt at sustainability, the great intellectual Ailton, of the Krenak people, offers an important reflection:
  So in this position as sponsors of our progress, these gentlemen believe they have the right to commit every kind of barbarity, including carrying out a genocide against the Kaiowá-Guarani people in Mato Grosso do Sul, justifying it by saying that this year they exported 200 million tons of grain, most of which is soy. It is monoculture, it uses poison, it poisons the water sources, the bodies of water, it poisons people directly, you don't even need to wait to drink the water afterward, you can just drink the poison straight away. And just because these people bring a few billion into the Brazilian economy, they believe they have the right to poison us. That's recolonization. To recolonize is exactly that. To recolonize is to bring in a demand that isn't ours, to export our water and our soil, to create poverty in these places, not to give these people the opportunity to establish themselves with dignity. And the most that is left for the neighbors of these enterprises is to be cheap labor, with the aggravating factor that the technologies applied today in this field, in this large-scale production, increasingly do without human labor and specialize in the use of machines,
  53
  of other expensive technologies that we don't manufacture, we buy. So we keep creating this circle of dependency, where indigenous peoples and the territories where indigenous peoples still manage to subsist are becoming almost the last strongholds where fauna and some biodiversity can survive (KRENAK, 2015, p. 333-334).
  In Kaiowá and Guarani territories, the forest and landscape diversity were almost completely destroyed by the karaí reko and by the colonialist political project, with the consolidation of the State and the creation of Indigenous Reserves for the expansion of the monopolization
  of land, of agriculture and livestock farming, and of agribusiness, especially from 1970 onward. This has shaped a broad process of ecosystem degradation, poisoning, fragmentation, insecurity, and territorial precarity for our people.
  In this narrative, the problems, conflicts, and violence faced by the Kaiowá and Guarani are closely related to the loss of a significant part of the tekoha, to the impositions of the enclosures represented by the Indigenous Reserves, to the profound territorial precarity and ecological degradation, and, consequently, to the need to meet most needs and carry out most work outside the village, since biodiversity in the traditional territory has been substantially reduced (BENITES, 2020).
  For this reason it is necessary to engage in dialogue and to better understand the workings of the internal and external policies that involve us, and thus to have clear objectives, since we indigenous people can only be sustainable once we have our territory back, in communion with spirituality. In this way it will be possible to reconquer our territory and thereby help Mother Earth in her natural resilience.
  I believe that if we understand that a leader can bring people together and change the human mind to the point of putting
  54
  their lives at the service of the struggle, as in the case of Sepé Tiaraju,6 a surprising reaction in the reconquest of our territories would be possible. The problem is that today we are unable to react to the system in which we are embedded, because we are guaxos, as Ñanderu Valério said in his words already quoted here.
  In the past, our leaders had voice and standing within and outside the community, but today, after the entry of the teko karaí (the non-indigenous way of being) into our midst, we disregard our elders, we seek instead to listen to what the karaí say, and thus we lose our customs, traditions, and spirituality, letting ourselves be
  6 Great Brazilian indigenous warrior, declared by law a "Guarani-Missionary hero of Rio Grande do Sul."
  contaminated by the capitalist system, leaving forgotten our teko joja (harmonious way of walking).
  In light of these reflections, it becomes clear that for there to be territorial sustainability, there must first be spiritual sustainability. If our spirits are healthy and joyful, if we are able to ensure our prayers, songs, rites, and celebrations, we will be able to maintain the Kaiowá and Guarani system of sustainability.
  **Food Sustainability**
  ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
  55
  Figure 3: Hunt. Personal archive.
  In indigenous wisdom, according to the elders, such as the late elder of Aldeia Panambizinho, Paulito Aquino, food defines people, such that you are what you eat. So, if you eat cassava that has been well planted and well blessed, it will also give you health, just as if you eat good corn, it will give health and joy to the body. This is because, for us indigenous people, everything is life, unlike the way the white man sees life. Production also comes from people, from the human, so production is human, corn is human, cassava is human, because it was produced by people, and so they also converse, speak to one another, and rejoice together (PERALTA, 2017).
  The stories told by Dona Odalícia, of the tekoha Panambizinho, about her childhood and adolescence here in the Dourados region, tell a little about the relationship between the diversity of life and good food in the past:
  We were sustainable, we had great abundance, food was never lacking no! There really was a lot of food, we were free and everyone had plenty of good food. There was no poison in the fields, we ate a lot of hu'i, lots of roasted sweet potato, cassava, fish, capybara, agouti. We had everything! I remember when we all used to go to the fields, grown-ups and children alike, there we played and worked at the same time. We harvested a lot of
  56
  food, rice, kumanda, acara, sweet potato, avati, and we would make a fire, roast avati, and eat a lot right there. In those days there was no mitã piru (malnourished child). Now here in Panambizinho has very few piru children, because we still have plenty of our own food and prayer too, but now there are already younger mothers, who don't want to make xixá for the children, nor make hu'i. They only eat what comes in the basic food basket, and that is bad food, it leaves us weak and sick. I miss when we used to go to the yguasu, we would pack provisions to eat along the road, we would go gathering guavirá, mbokaja, mixirica fruits. There was plenty of pakowá, we would gather a lot of fish, a whole lot! We would stay there five, six days. Afterward we would return to the tekoha. There wasn't even a fence, it was all open, but, then the karaí arrived and started closing everything off. We could no longer even go in to fish, or gather fruit, everything was torn away, the forest, our fields, everything was finished... (tears). My father used to say that now was a hard time and that we had to pray. We were confined to 60 ha, after much struggle we got back part of our tekoha, but already there is no more forest, nor animals. Everything is finished! I think the work you all are doing will help my great-grandchildren and the family have more good food. Agwyjevete. (Odalícia Concianza - in memory- of Panambizinho).
  That is how my people were: rich in food and medicine. We did not depend on the market, on pharmacies, we had everything, as shown by the testimony of this woman who kept the good moments of our people in her memory. In this way, I think that today's generations
  suffer the consequences of this so-called economic development, for it is a generation that grew up without space to live its teko porã (good living). It is a generation that grew up *being un-wrapped [des-envolvidos] from its food customs — that* is, stripped of its way of being, living, and eating. They learned to value industrialized foods, which has caused hunger, malnutrition, and other health problems.
  Fostering the possibility of carrying out the prayers for preparing the soil, for planting and harvesting in the communities involved would be a way of leading the
  ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
  57
  generations to once again acquire the habit of cultivation and the sustainable management of the tekoha. To carry out this training in awareness and in the strengthening of the individuals involved, and thus to produce healthy food free of poisons.
  Food sustainability, known as sustainable food production, or as conservation agriculture, is one of the main objectives to be achieved in agriculture. Conservation agriculture seeks to learn from nature, where everything in the system is kept in balance and everything works in harmony. However, production systems that work with the conservation of ecosystems have been one of the greatest challenges for communities in recent decades.
  From this perspective, several studies have shown that food sustainability is a viable goal, and that through the effort and dedication of the agricultural community it is possible to reach this objective. Our indigenous people, with our way of producing food developed ancestrally, in a harmonious and balanced manner, can point the way toward a new relationship with agriculture and food sovereignty.
  **Environmental Sustainability**
  58
  Figure 4: Xiru Karaí, at Tekoha Panambizinho. Source: Xiru Karaí Archive.
  Environmental sustainability is the key piece that closes the cycle of the discussions made so far, since the environment is the place that shelters, feeds, and helps give life to us humans and the other beings that make up the scene of Mother Earth. The environment is capable of suffering drastic aggressions and still benefiting us. However, its resilience does not operate on human time, and in recent times we have seen and heard, among all the native peoples and scientists, that the world is in collapse.
  We see leaders across the whole world giving environmental speeches, setting goals to be reached, and trying to soften climate effects, but little is seen in practice to improve the planet's quality of life. And the people who are most affected by the environmental destruction caused by the non-indigenous way of living are precisely the peoples who live in the greatest connection with life in their territories. This is what is called environmental racism.
  Western society has wrapped people up in a way of thinking and acting that produced a "consumer society," in which all the wealth of the planet can be extracted to benefit a small group of the human population. They deforest, they pollute the rivers, they destroy mountains, they dig up the soil. All of this in the name of so-called
  progress. And in the midst of all this, what is left to us is a wounded environment, saddened, shaken by the greed of karaí reko (the white way of living). White people call this development [desenvolvimento], and in a way they are right, because in our view, this so-called development means removing the involvement [envolvimento] from relationships, since the prefix "des-" means separation, negation.
  59
  In a healthy environment we can live without so many economic expenses, we have our food and medicines available, with equity, respect, and care among all living beings. This way of thinking may seem like utopia to Western, capitalist society, but it was in exactly this way that our ancestors lived for millennia, in harmony and communion.
  In this way, we indigenous peoples have applied, since our existence began, the ideas of sustainability, which take into account the harmony between ecosystems and societies; in such a way that we do not exhaust the riches of nature, we treat the environment with respect, we seek a balance between what we take and what we offer in return, and we consider that our planet is one, and that every action affects the whole, for life is interaction and everything is interrelated.
  As the Kaiowá researcher Isaque João points out, in the traditional Kaiowá and Guarani system of environmental management, the gathering of roots and fruits was always guided by the Ñanderu and Ñandesy so as not to provoke the displeasure of the jara (owners), and the strength of the hexakáry's (seer's) prayer was what protected the collective, attracted game animals, and maintained the fertility of the kokuê (cultivated field), making it possible to find the best place to live amid all the biodiversity (JOÃO, 2011). These relations establish a harmonic dynamic among ecology, territory, and ancestral spirituality.
  From this point of view, the reflections of the great shaman Davi Kopenawa alert us to the power of this interaction of life, in which we bear great responsibility for the care of all existing life:
  The forest is alive. It will only die if white people insist on destroy- ing it. If they succeed, the rivers will disappear beneath the earth, the ground
  will come undone, the trees will wither, and the stones will crack from the *heat. The parched earth will be left empty and silent. The xapiri spirits, who*
  60
  come down from the mountain to play in the forest in their mirrors, will flee far away. Their fathers, the shamans, will no longer be able to call them and make them dance to protect us. They will not be able to drive away the smoke of epidemic that devours us. They will no longer manage to contain the evils, which will turn the forest into chaos. Then we will die, one after another, white people and us alike. All the shamans will end up dying. When there is no longer a single one of them alive to hold up the sky, it will fall (KOPENAWA and ALBERT, 2009, p. 6).
  For us, Guarani and Kaiowá, caring for and managing the environment we live in is a social and spiritual duty, and our traditional agriculture allows the land to feed itself over a long period, so that it may recover its vigor, germinating again through the presence and agency of the jára. According to the Kaiowá anthropologist Celuniel Valiente, in this process, care is needed in managing the environment, taking great care not to affect the space of the other human; understanding that humans are many, not only those considered as such by the karaí's view (VALIENTE, 2019).
