  Looking at the environment from a spiritual approach, as we indigenous peoples do, one notices that the source of change lies in inner strength. A spiritually conscious people will accept its responsibility in this chain of events and will take a stand to protect life and keep the sky from falling. For us indigenous peoples, discussing internally and with the surrounding society the importance of Mother Earth's resilience, and our role in preserving and caring for the environment, will turn this failing world into a new world: fully alive and healthy.
  To close this chapter, I have brought the words of Dona Marilda Duarte, Ñandesy of the Dourados village, who honored me with a visit to the Xiru Karaí, Panambizinho, on September 13, 2019, bringing a holistic and critical Kaiowá and Guarani view on Mother Earth and on the need for us to work on our Kaiowá
  61
  and Guarani sustainability. I will present the text first in the Guarani language and then I will interpret her narrative.
  Mba’éixapa enterovéva amombe’úta moõpa paiko. Xe réra Marilda Duarte, aiko aldeia Douradospe, Bororópe, amorá. Entonces xe tupã réra Kunhã Poty Rendy amoite ivanga arapoite xe réra ikunhã Oká Poty Rendy.
  Entonces yvy rehegwa, yvy pyte rehegwa yvy pytã nhõarupi yvy oĩ ja, do outro ladia moyvy só que peteĩ, peteĩ maerãpe pa nhã’ẽ pe ikatu tavyterã guarani opaixagwa natureza, nhande tekohápe, entonces pe yvy maranã’ỹ rehegwa nhanderu Ty’apy Guasu, ha’e ojapo jave pe ko nhande planetarã ha’e mba’yre entonces ha’e ou ko yvýre opyta ha’e ou ko uvýre opyta entonces upéa oikotamo ko yvy ha’e ndoikatúi oiko ko yvýre ha’e ndaikatúi nhanderu. Entonces he’i, nhandesýpe Xiru Pa’i Kwara sýpe ha’i poty mirĩ sýpe, pe ha’i sy mirĩ sýpe he’i grávida xugwy ha ndaikatumo’ãi oraha hendie ojapo hagwa rógape.
  Upépe ndaikatumo’ãi, nhaikatumo’ãi, oiko onhondive, marãmo ha’e ohóta japo róga yvága rapýpe ko’ãga oĩ hagwa ha’e upémarõ pe yvy ha’e oheja nhadévepe ndaikatu jaiko hagwa, nhandekwera, Paĩ Tavyterã kwéra je entero mi víxo kwéra oiko hagwa yvy pepe. Só que ha’e omoĩ heta mba’e nhandéve rekorã ojeha nhande principalmente Xiru Pa’i Kwara ko yvy reko katu maranã’ỹ hagwa nhande, primera cosa ja’éta hína nhamongueta itỹmbire, itỹmbire ha’e ojeha nhandéve mbo’itypa heja mba’eixapa nde ka’arurã hagwa, oiko, entonces upéa mba’égwy ko yvýgwy oiko, ko yvýgwy oiko onasce ojaty, ojaty ikatu hagwaixa, onasce.
  Entonses ha’ekwéra omombe’uha la dia, mba’eixapa ha’ekwéra ko yvy ojapoarã nhande hagwaete, etezia peve ha’e reko katu maranẽ’ỹ hagwa oje oiko hagwa kunhã ndéve ko yvy cada ano ha’ekwéra ohero ko yvy mba’eixapa cada ano ohero ko
  62
  yvy cada ano ovela ombo’a vevo pe yvy katu haixagwa jajaty javehyupy nhande rembi’urã ovy’a hagwaixa pe itỹmbyre, ha’e cada ano ohero pe yvy. Ohasáva pe yvy ha’e porã serõ upeagwy.
  Entonses upéa pe yvy nhonhemorõi oĩ mo’õpa ha’e hovasa hagwérõ pe três dias apeve yvy ha onhemo’e ramo mba onhemo’eramo yvy oĩ harapeso que ka’agwy mbyterope oĩ hesaya apeka cada ka’agwy pauraipy umi nhupa ureĩpe oĩ vae opa ko’ãga yvy y secopa ndorekói he’i mbayre nẽ’ẽ sadia veima pe yvy porque ka’agwy, ka’agwýre la opyrũ, cada pyhare tem ohosãmaikatu hagwaixa ha’e oguereko comunidade yvýpe nhande hagwa peivy porã hagwape ejaty akwe otera ka’agwy opaixagwa mi onace mi maerã. Ha ndaipóri ka’agwy jaety paete ojere kokwe guasu, maramõ opyta peagwy yvy ha’e oĩ rendépe ndahekokatúi maranẽ’ỹ ndorekói ndovy’ái ha’e.
  Entonses renhonotỹrejajatiramõ se me tỹgwe ha’e ja no po’ĩ porã véima entonses upéi pe oĩma ha’ekwéra heta ojapo yvy rehe oĩma adubo je ha opamba’e ojapo xupe porque depois quando nascer véima naturalmente. Nhande causa o seco, resseca jepeka ka’agwyetypa marãmo o sinai ndoyveima ha upéixa ko’ãga ne umi tekoharepe ... ndakatúi nhande itermina iterei ka’agwy katui jetepe ka’agwy jajety véima yvyra kwéra ikatu hagwã ogweru jey upéa ka’agwýre, porã ka’agwyre, oĩ mbejo, oĩ nhũ, opaixagwa pohãiterei, pohã, pire, yvyra mata, peteĩ pire ha’e ombongwera hagwe ereru arã ndahaira momboaty ypohíra eterei, pera upea ... ogweru porã umi yvy nembo’egwere porã oĩhápe mba’asy nhande ... ikatu nhande rasy’i ipohĩma mba nde ramo mbotyra nhande tekoha como pohã ka’agwy pegwa seco pegwa, brexo pegwa, nde rerimboty ramo ikatu hagwáicha imbogwera e tekoha yva verde porque pohã pyre ha’e re’u rekai’u urembote’y ore, oĩ nde rasyete ramo, oĩ kwera, oĩ ikatu nhande rasy alguém machuca alguna cosa oĩ nhande kwéra jakwera voíre, voíre ogweraha oĩ zias kwera porãi hagwa ha upéi
  63
  jave nderekói porãi tereré, rekai’u, rekai’u, rekai’u urei, como ainda reimba iporã pyre pohãrungwe oĩre hagwã ha nderekwaaiva árupi ndaikwavéima pohã rogwe como pohã pyre ramo.
  Pe nũpegwa pohã oĩ, oĩ héra avápe mamangá upe mbohaxa gwýpe yvyra mbohaxa gwýpe, yvyra upéa ha’e iporã rekai’u hagwã xupe, iporã kunhã ikyravape avei; py’a he'i ko hasy aje ora iporã ai
  iporã kai hagwã se ha iko rejapo pe mbohaxa xugwy pulando pytã ivai je ai ha upea iporã yve ha’e câncer, câncer de utero he’e mba’yre aje mamangá he’e xupe mba’eixa pomba’yre renhõi po ha’e ha mbejo pegwa katui ha’e heta eterei oĩ ohaisande ndaikwaai oheja mbejo kunhã pyrũ mba’eve ... mbejope katu oĩ porã ysã opaixagwa pohã kunhã como jajajereko aikwa ramo pegwa heta ha’e porque oĩ mamo jei tei jei ko haropy opaixagwa pira é nhande ikatu já utiliza nhanhã pira, pira rampinha, pira juruaija, pira pochi, tarairá opaixagwa pira umia oje’u só que upe já’ua eikwe ã nde repo nderehe ainte ndere upei kunhã taí, como mitã guasu, ha omendadarã ha ojegwatase oje cria ha’e aje.
  Entonses upéa rehe okokumatará tembi’ukwe he’i ymagware. Mba’eixapa ha’e popota esse ou remondiá upea, entoses kunhã kyra já memby ja’e membypa rire entonses upéa pegwa mbejo rupi ha’e porã oĩ, oĩ rea upea remõi roesape oho he’u hagwãixa mboje, mbojeĩma ha’u hagwã oĩ brexope, ysyrýpe péixa osyry jave oĩ upea rehe otyky oho’a upea kaatu oĩma yvy are ndeve rehema oĩma upea katui py’a rupu porã e a pressão oĩma pohã indaikatui sofre a pressão enterovea jareko pressão aje. Entonses upea pegwa ha’e oĩ ave tarova rehe oho opovy’aruarem he oho, arẽ upea epy’a epy’a pohã pressão pohã, hate ysyry opyky vae opeivarẽ y arenyve he oho itárovare osyry upea ikatu hũ porã coraçõ asipe, nde coraçõ mancha pende
  64
  coraçõpe.
  Entonses onhẽgogwera upea tuixa mba’e coraçõ tuixa, primeiro lugar hina, nde ha ela é voluntário, oĩ ndeve coraçõ upea pohã ohopeíre istriri avei oho itárovare tei oho ahina upe porã na missão, heta eterei oĩ pohã brexo pengwarã ja’úta nhande kwera, nhande kwera, porque nhandekwera ta ikatu tayterã, jareko gwa’e ke pressão nde re’u, jajereko nhacontrolado ja’u jajereko he’i mba’yre aje ai ja jarekopama hagwã oi, só que upéa arive oĩ opy’a oĩ mbarete rehe ope opeririá te ... aje upe’au pohã controlado pegwa é na mesma hora de johesa’y rehegwe pererokoi. Entonses mba’apo ne kane’õ ka’aru ramo nhamõi ikatu maraike nde participa ne nhenhamõi nde py’a ko piriri piriri, entonses opea pegwa porã oĩ isã oĩ brexo umia ha’e brexo pegwa ha ose’i.
  Ai ka’agwy jyvaete are nhamoĩta hína porã mba’yrehe ýpe anemia ha’i anemia ha’i kunhã nderugwe nderehe pa’y nde mba’asy mẽ’ẽ aje nde ka’agwyre nde oho e upea iporã yvotyrã naimoãi veima ha jaremoĩma, eremoĩma yvyra pytã pire, ha remoĩma irunde pire, repy’a retoraí irunde’i pire pono que ne mbarete ha nde vare’a hagwã. Ape hendy’e pe kankoroza aje kankoroza, cachorro ha remõi poheia.
  Huvixa moyremoirã, ophã guasu, huivixa moyremõi ko’anga omombe’uta xirixaha ko, ko pohã teĩ porãiterei peãga ohendu rogwe pe ary pe kagware guasu rugwaigwe rehapy ipo’y ipo’y umi oĩ aje. Entonses rejara upearã hapy ha nde renhõi pupu arã pe ela huvixa anemia porã, hapyka ora poré moía randivepe, apohã guasu hina pea peteĩ pohã ija’e nhnade xupe peteĩ grupo, peteĩ pohã itirapáva nhãnẽ’ẽ etepe aje itirapáva pea peteĩ pea seco ka’agwy rehegwa meme hina upea pió servi asy anemia pepe o servi pohã iterei.
  65
  Ome’ẽ primeira cosa nhande ogwereko he’i ko ha’ekwera aje xe ko omombe’uta pe’eme heí ha’ekwera aiko aje, aje nhamõi, nhande reko jara ivaikwe nhandeve. Entonses há’e upeixa aje yvy peypota jeiramo heí oime hapeterei pe mombo’e mba’ekwe hopi hagwã mba’era ihy upi umia jevyaramo pe’eme, entoses, nhande jajaty ha ka’agwyre jei nhambopoky.
  Mba’eixa nacomeça nhambohary hagwã, entonses ko’ape oĩ Arroyo aje, com Arroyo kota koi ndoikoi ka’agwy apenas amoite mixĩ oĩ ka’agwy, entonses ko ikontare direito já jaty hagwã mba’ere 500 metros nederredor japoa rã ka’agwy jaty, jaty paite irunde’i, yvyra pytã, jatobá, oĩ agwyer (?) até umi yva já’u aje ha’u ikatu hangwãixa e sombra ha ousã ha upeare ikatu hangwãixa ha upeixala yvy jara. Nhande kwera ko ja’iu yhyjaregwarei nhande ja’iu ipemina própria na ja’iu.
  Outro ha’e ko y peteĩ outro mundo ndaha’ei ha’e nhande kwera, nhande, nhande mundo por causa que nhande, nhande já respirá, nhande, nhande pytũhẽ ko hape ha amoite upejaike ... pytũhẽ upepe outro mundo, nhanderu, nahdesy kaja’a ha hente poxi, nda ha’ei, hente marangatu upea gwima omõimina nde pepe
  peteĩ ivarte pe’y ha tomina mitã taí hotera ha emoimĩ pene akaja pypyme nde pe quanta hora?
  Pea heiko jajaka pe ype aje ndarekoi na haĩ nda... Enstonses pe jajuka. Upe’a é Xiru nhamòi kaja’a há’ekwera nhanderu, hoga pei osyry peivae, ha’ekwera nhanderu hoga pei osyry peivae, ai mundo, ha nhande já’iú arã ipeagwy oĩ amoite mina gwygware inhandejairoga.
  Upeixa ... jaihuí ha roga jajejaíúramo entonses upea ha roga’i mesma coisa kunhã nhandereko ape carpi nhande roga aje, então upeixa ha’ekwera oĩ o carpi’i oga aje. Ha ha’ekwera moãi ore ko ha’ekwera rimba heta ave ore ko mesma cosa nhande oga
  66
  pegwa...
  Ha’ekwera rimba nhandesy ka’ajaha nhanderu ka’ajala ore ko ha’e rimba kokwetiu ndorekoi jacaré, ha`e ogwereko sucuri`y, umia arroyo opa onhatumba ore oiko aje ha’ekwera ha’e minha ogwareko umia je upeagwy jaha mombyry ha rupi iteko ihaupy mongajaramo vixo ipoxi aje, entose ha’ekwera umia ha’ekwuea ... tekoha move’ade tekoha move’ade. Entose, pe’y entonse ha’e nhandekwera ndorekoi direito guasu veima oĩ nhande pa peagwy opa pe ndorekoi direito jejaty oĩ ka`agwy 500 metros emredor da mina jerera ha como Arroyo jerera. Porque nhande javyaveiry ko yvy pipe por causa nhande ko jahei jaieterei nhade rekovia je, nhnadereko haveje nde reko haja hejaiterei nhanhomõi ete, gwasuveimave. Entonse Xiru Paí Kwara nhande resa pe ha reiko nhanhendui nhẽgaraje, upe ava Poty rusu nhohendui nhẽgara ha’i jejupe. Entonses nhanderu teapu guasu tekojara nhã ne nhadepohu, ha ĩmimbo’ei é como nda rapekwaha ha’ekwera cada ka’aru, ou seja, cada sábado nhande taí katu jareko direito já nhanbo onha mbaraka, nhamborahei hagwã nhadereko oĩava, nhnadereko kwyávo ndarekoi katu marana`ỹ vaerã ai ha’ekwerra ndaindarekoi. Sim xe areko peteĩ tekoja, xe mboruvare opuraheiva oga guasupe amoite yvangara pypegwa xe monhagareko ka va’ekwe, xe ayvu omonhangareko ka oharehe hente ogwahẽ xe aresevy. Xe upea xe xe kovajara amoite, xe anhendu araẽ enterro teko jaragwy oĩ teko jaratejapy guasu nhanderu teko guasu oĩ nhandesy marangatu, oĩ
  nhandesy mandereiju kanindé, oĩ nhaderu guarani kaninndé mandereiju kanindé, oĩ verá ponĩ ha’ekwera nhanderru ha nhandesy ha’ekwera oĩ tekojá oĩ nhande, nhande reko jara anhemo’ãrusũ nhanderu, anhemo’ãrusũ oĩ nhande jajereko nhande rejo ave, nhande reko jara ha inha he’i mba’yre nhande haixa rusu, nhande jareko, haixa teko aresã sãkare onhagareko

  nhandejareko. Upea nhẽgá nhandai nhamboekwarã dai, dai nhãnhãdai peteĩ tekojara nhande jajehu paite atekojaragwy nhemboekenha Xiru Pai Kwará nhẽkarava ava potỹ nhẽkara nde rupi’a. nde rejehu ara ave umĩ ikatu nhãkweragury, umĩ okakwe, umĩ ha’ekwera ogwereko pra nhanderu te ave.

Entonse oĩandereko jara ape ara vai, ara vai, avaikwera, ava poriahu he’i ha’ekwerave, he`ekwera ojei oĩ temporalpe ha nhandeve ituixa ha’ekwera oje’i ovyrãmo hina nde roga oĩ typoí ho’u aje. Nhnade jareko avary ke’yrusu anhã Fifi, nhande jareko avary ke’yrusu anhangare’i nhnade jareko avary ke’yrusu’i ele kaitereiva oĩ gwanhãgwapy nhande jagwareko gwanhãgwapy mba’egwy nhande jara upea anhãgwapy, ha anhã Fifi, avarike irusu anhãgware, ha’ekwera omoĩnhadeve yvytu nhande pytũ hagwã.
  Ko yvytu omoĩ nhaandeve ko ary nhandejara respira hagwã, upea vae nde reuni ãgwarekwape nhandeve, entose umĩa kwera nhegára peteĩ opurahei onhandesy, onhanderu otera mitã’ĩ ohe como potĩ mbojerroky va’ekwe yvyrayjá, jai nhande xupe. Nhande jaipe nda ndive ape nhanderu hape nda ndive nhandesy pea hape mitã ojehe kombu’e agwapy (?) yvyrayjá nhandejara, só que nhande entero eui yvyrayjá tenho só que pei arando jaiporã cetero ha’e ogwerekovei oĩ opaixagwa teko, upeagwy jerejorovya umĩa teko jarakwera re he`i entose nem maestro tamem boa escuela porã oĩ enm maética hãngwãixa reigwarẽ upe ikatu hangwãixa reiko arupyty, umĩ vae teko. 68 Jareko arupy ta xe reko arupyty xe rendirá e he’i mondeve nde rikwa’ai, nde upearã nde, nde reikwa’aimoãi, mboescuela monde ikwa’ata tá xe kwarupyty na xe revyra’e, xe reko johuna, xe revyra’e ta xe reko johuna, xe nde re mondeve entonses upe nhẽ’ẽ nderekoi hangwãixa ndereíxa hangwãixa mba’eixapa nde. Nhnade kwera yvyópra nha ndajerekoi 500 anos de vida, nhandekwera yvypóra jareko apenas 100 anos de vida, muito menos nde japoraveima de la cosa, na nhemba’ererovy`a erro ndarekoi mba’eramo. Nhnade jareko mokõi tape, nhnade paí já tape vai upyto aipa jaikotá ota tape, tape porã entonse upea nhande kwera jarekotá ikatui. Nhande he aje he’i mba`yre nhẽ’ẽpe tem hora que nhande, nhande carne fraca jajereko aije, mas só que muito menos nde repensar em primeiro lugar hese mba’eixapa nde reko ta yvy peixa, jeko ha’u nhande kwera jareko mante cimi paí ikatu, como kaiowá e guarani, mba’yre pa jerokotá kwa’a kunhã je jehe por causa que nhande, nhande kwera paí katu ser humano aguentaí mba’asy jajerovy amamante.
  Mbo xeajehu jave areko este ãnho opurahei va’ekwe Bororópe o tal de câncer herave nhanderru va’ekwe na mama e o cuiahaixa ha’e ojeroky o xe rundi’e ndatatui. Entonse ha xe reko jave sete ãnhos xe jeroky moãi primeira coisa xa jeroky okwe takwa, jeroky, jeroky upeixa aiko xe tua ha maioria he’e mba’yre je epe xixá xe conhece jerosy, ojapo jerosy puku avati morõntĩ pei tymbire, peixivi nhamõi jakairá, po ojapo va’ekwe jerosy ahexa ko arekoi siete anho omorava eikwe glevape herave e nhanderu Paulito rembyreko avei, entose upea xa e xa ko’apo mante rosy...
  Entonse até que agwahẽpeve xe, xe amenda hapyta, xe mãmondi’e xe nda hexai, xe sy vangará pegwa mante, xa reko jeve cinco ãnhos xe, xe sy janhemaĩna, janhe ndimaĩna ndaikwa’ai je pe xupe entonse xe kakwa’a xe tio, xe tia.
  69
  Ai sim, upeagwy ahesa um tempão aheja mba’yre é hangwã upeagwy xe ani envolver areko jave, xe dezesseis anos, xe ani envolverma mborahei aprofundar hangwã, ani envolver ahexa
  hangwã mba’egwypa nhande, nhande omano mba’e mba’eixapa nhande jaiko arã mba’egwypa. Entose upiá upepe assim mba’ery ofoca oĩ xe, xe re kõ akyre mba’egwype nhande ojo, ojohe japoko mba’eixa jaiko jei ko harupi upeixa oĩ xe araha há atopala nhande sy Dona ha’e oĩme ko’anga noivixa... oĩme aldeia sucuri’ype ndoivixa porã veima oporandu... Dona entonse ha ela xe maestro akwe ha’e ha imena xe exa jeroky siete ãnhos, siete ãnhospe aje jeroky upepe lá xe ha otopa xe sy a como se ru.
  Ome'ẽva xeve ko'ẽ ha ka'akru, conselho xe rekorã haxy mba'e porandu ixupe mba'eixapa teikorã. Ha upeagwy he'i xeve ha'e acredita ahexama avei mombe'u pire aje, entonse ko'anga rupy ramo nhanhamboy keyramo nhande reko, õ entregama javei servicio oreve ojeroky 50 familias rendi'e durante sete ãnhos, orombo jojahãngwa ore, ore rekoha jeroky he'i o se um maestro ko'anga ha'e três zias peixa mandu'a mba'epa xeve oĩme nhande sy rã peteĩ te nhande mba'opea oĩme nhande rura peteĩ te nhande mba'apaõpea estezia teko jara duas horasouta omombo joja nẽ'ẽ nhandive ha upepe pe'ẽ mbojojatape nẽ'ẽ. mbava e repeikota pe'ẽpe moitá nẽ'ẽ renonde ha ko'ẽ ramo gwarã upeipe peiko hangwã he'i aje. Entonses iporã he'i oreve upeia ha entonse he'ixe ko he'i xe roga ape roga ha xe outro oga e mama (?) hape porahei oyta he'i aje, ha poanxa teko rehe oĩ he'ira e a ha'e oreve araka'e aje ndo ropytai ... noutro aldeiape peixa ore mborahei pea. Entonse upeixa ... jaiko acerto upea ha'e... outra aldeia jei tempão japo rupi serviço memo, memo pe oia ogwe ko sempre okora haje. Entonse oreve eteziasgwe jejoja nẽ'ẽ ẽrõ ko'arã crente (Marilda Duarte, Bororó). Transcription by Chamirĩ Kwatia Verá Rendyju.
  70
  She begins her account like this: How are you all? My name is Marilda Duarte, I live in the Bororó village, which is in Dourados. My name up in the sky is Kunã Poty Rendy. We came from the middle of this land, both the Guarani and the Kaiowá, we are all from the same place. Our tekoha is this red earth, for in other places it is already different.
  When God made this land, He did not stay here. He said to our mother and to the mother of the Great Sun God: "I made this sacred land for the Xiru Paí Kwará, so I cannot stay here on this land," and so He left us here and rose up to the sky to make His home there. He left this land here for us, human beings, and for all the species of animals and plants. He left many things for us, above all the sacred land, which was the first thing, but He also left the seed full of spirit, for us to eat. Without these foods we would not be able to live, for the seeds have always been born from the earth. So all one has to do is plant, just as He did. God, every year, baptizes the earth by sending the frost, and in this way it becomes new and fertile each year. With the frost He performs the baptism of the earth so that it produces food well.
  The earth is no longer well, because they have put an end to the forests. Today there are no longer springs the way there used to be, everything has already dried up. Our land no longer has health. It is in the woodland where He walks that the earth is cooled, because the dew falls, and so the earth has moisture so that the seed can be born well, but with the felling of the forest, the earth is no longer happy, it no longer has joy, that is why there is now drought, that is why we have to plant tree seedlings.
  We need the woodland, it is there that we seek out medicines, there is medicine in the bark of the trees. If the illness is not very strong, it heals, but if the illness is very strong we have to add more of the wood's bark, mix it all together, and drink it. If the illness is very strong, mix all the medicines of the
  71
  woodland, of the marsh, and then you will heal. You take the medicine's bark in mate, in tereré, to heal quickly. If something is hurting, sometimes you don't heal fast, it can take up to ten days to heal well. That is why we have to keep drinking tea made from the leaves, the bark, the medicine. Now many people no longer know anything about the medicines.
  In the fields we have many medicines, one is called mamanga, the fig tree, the sap of the fig tree. Drinking it in mate is very good for a pregnant woman, so that the child is not slow to be born, so that she does not suffer. This medicine looks like rubber, it is good for cancer of the
  uterus. In the marsh there is also a lot of cooling medicine, when we go into the marsh we walk right over the medicine and we don't know what medicine is in the marsh. There are various cooling medicines there for women.
  If a young person, whether man or woman, eats the wrong things, depending on what is eaten it can bring suffering. For example, if one eats certain fish like traíra, catfish, piranha, when the time comes to have a child, there will be great suffering. It is the same with the marsh medicines, you cook them and drink them in running water where it drips at the edge of the bank. That is where the good medicines for a racing heart are found. This medicine is for those with high blood pressure. This medicine sits on top of the stones and passes into the earth, it is a great medicine, it goes into the water too. We have all the medicines that help us and that we can drink so as not to fall ill. We have illnesses that frighten us, but if we take these medicines properly, everything passes, and then you can go back to work. You worked, at night you are already tired, you lie down and cannot sleep, your chest is tight, frightened, it is sick, but in the marsh there is medicine.
  72
  There is medicine also in the tall woodland. The karaí speaks of anemia, we say that our blood turns to water, and for this the medicine cannot be bark alone, one must add the bark of the canafístula, the bark of the aroeira, burned and toasted, so that it doesn't become too strong and harsh, so that it gives an appetite. Everyone knows these medicines, one also adds nó-de-cachorro. These are the leading medicines. One also adds the tail of the kanguare, but it is boiled separately, and also the picão. All these medicines are for treating anemia, this mixture of various barks is to make one strong. These medicines are all from the tall, dry woodland.
  With the loss of the forest we need to plant, because the owner of our life said that if we want a renewed land we need to sow, to plant the seed of the forest again. Here, for example, we have the stream, and along its banks there is no longer any forest. Only far off in the back there is a small patch of woodland, so we have to plant around it canafístula, aroeira, jatobá, whatever fruits we eat. That way we will have shade, it will stay cool, and the water and its owner will rejoice.
  The water has an owner, we only drink water from above, we do not drink from the spring of the original source. This original water is from another world, it is not from our world, because we breathe. There, we do not breathe, in that water over there it is another world. Our father, our mother, and the mermaid are very fierce beings, they are not sacred beings. So that you understand, put water in a bucket, a child comes and falls in face down. That child can even drown and die quickly, because water has no branch to hold on to, it kills you fast. This is Xiru nhamõi kaja'a, it is the world of the waters. It is their world. That is why they do not drink this water, the running water is the world of the kaja'a mermaids and we drink there from the spring. It is from there that we must drink, so that we
  73
  will not drink from their house.
  For example, here is a house of grass, and their house is like that too. They have many animals, nhanderu kaja'a and nhandesy kaja'a, there is alligator, anaconda, fish. Everything that lives in the water are their animals, they are the ones who care for these animals. On dry land all the animals also have an owner, that is how they are. They are the owners of all the animals that live in the water, but the water is running out, that is why they are not happy, because all the woodlands are being felled. It's just that we have the right and the duty to plant the forest again around the streams and at the springs.
  We are no longer happy because we are abandoning our culture, our way of being. The Xiru Kwará is no longer hearing our prayers, our songs, the ava Potyrusu is no longer listening to our voice. They are sad with us.
  In the old days, we prayed every day, today that no longer happens. We no longer have the teko jara. I have the teko jara, the one who sings up in the sky. He sent me to care for people. I receive all the people who come to me, I do not listen only to the people of my own teko jara, I have to listen to all the teko jara in order to be a caretaker of lives.
  There are several teko jara hy’apyguasu, there is ñandesy marangatu, there is ñandesy mande reju, there is kanindé, there is nhanderu guarani, kanindé marindeju, there is vera ponhy nhanderu and nhandesy of the teko jara. There is teko jara anhemoã rusu nhanderu. We have our queen haxaruasu, we have hacha teko, who takes care of us, with her prayer. We
  ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
  74
  cannot exclude any teko jara, we all stand beside the teko jara, we cannot abandon them. All those who went there are the ñanderu, we need to keep in contact with them, because they know and understand the prayers. They communicate among themselves.
  75
  We also have the one who takes care of the storms that come knocking everything down, there are those who take care of our breath, there is a prayer for that too. It may be a ñandesy who cleanses the body of the youngest one who dances, the yvyraija. We are all yvyrayja, only those, the oldest men or women, are the wise ones, and it is in them that we need to believe, in this teko jara. Your teacher must teach you well so that you may reach that point, so that you may attain the sacred, and for this reason, you do not learn only from the teaching you receive. We attain this formation of life so that we may live well. If you do not believe in *yourself, you may suffer (Marilda Duarte, Bororó).*
  76
  **Seeds, Land, and Living Well: Kaiowá and Guarani Spiritual Technologies**
  The purpose of this part of the book is to discuss our Kaiowá and Guarani spiritual technology as epistemic knowledge, which, in my view, is ignored by the so-called civilized world. I will thus continue the reflections on the sustainability of life discussed in the previous chapter, and in this present chapter I will focus on three axes: seeds, the tekoha, and living well.
  At the outset, it is important to note that these axes are treated as sacred beings, as possessors of spirits, and, from the perspective of Kaiowá and Guarani sustainability, I will guide the reflections on the importance of these axes for maintaining our way of existing in the world, and on the care we must take so that the seeds, the land, and our living well may multiply with quality, so that the perpetuation of species and of beings becomes possible, in an environment with healthy life on this planet that came to be called Earth.
  First, it is important to recall, together with our elder women and men, the ancient times, when our people were free from colonizing evil. In ancient times, to make a field, there was an entire ritual, both in the preparation of the soil and in the planting of the seeds. Today, however, few people prepare their land in the traditional way. All the work of the field was organized by family groups, each with its own role. The men prepared the soil and planted, while the women and children tended and harvested. Traditionally there was (and still is) an appropriate month and moon, both for planting and for harvesting.
  There was a particular way of storing the traditional seed for the following year’s planting. It was knowledge that had to be
  77
  followed, passed down through the teachings of the elders, from generation to generation. This communal work was carried out only within
  family contexts, in the form of puxirõ (mutirão, collective labor). It was common among the older Kaiowá and Guarani to call people together to carry out work that required many hands.
  The factor underlying this system is unity, Kaiowá and Guarani spirituality. Because it is communal, it cannot be done alone. When we were created to admire the earth, not everything was ready-made; it was necessary to create the things that the mba’ejára (owners of beings) left for us, especially food, and that is why we gathered together singing so that the foods we needed would be born. It was by singing for long hours that Avati Morotĩ (white corn) was born, which my ancestors cared for as if it were a child. To this day people sing to gladden it, so that there may be a good harvest.
  In ancient times, Mother Earth herself required the Guarani and Kaiowá to live and work together, since the circumstances of the time demanded this form of bond in order to carry out hunting and planting. Just as a tree alone cannot survive healthy and happy, still less can human beings. That is why the Kaiowá and Guarani seek to live together, both in festivals and rituals and in work, which has the harvest and celebration as its purpose. It is in this context that we seek, in the elders who still pray, the inspiration to strengthen the young people and the whole community, so that they may be as productive as their ancestors were.
  **Seeds: A Source of Life and Resistance**
  Seeds are living beings, full of life, full of secrets, and full of the sacred. During this research of mine, it became very clear that
  78
  seeds are the beings responsible for the perpetuation of species and of all living beings of the spiritual world, within the cosmic world of which we are a part. They possess a complex spiritual technology capable of dying and reviving, of bearing fruit and feeding the other living species of planet Earth.
  For us Kaiowá, full life will only exist if seeds continue to exist, but for that we need to think of ways to recover our territories, so that we can practice our way of being and living, which is interconnected with the beings and spirits that inhabit the cosmos alongside our existence and with whom we maintain the communion of life. The seed is our source of strength and sustenance, and it is responsible for the human essence. In this way, it holds within its spirituality the continuity of life, of the most varied species, and sustains all other beings. The seed is the source of the sustainability of life.
  The word semente [seed], in the Portuguese language, comes *from the Latin sementis,7 and refers both to the seed of a fruit and* to any cause that permits the creation of something. Thus, the term seed is applied to the creation of life, of a fruit, or of an individual, but is not used in a strictly biological sense; it allows us to understand the origin of vital processes and indicates that in the cycles of nature there is always an originating cause, that is, a germ.
  In dialogue with Mr. Jorge Gomes, a leader and Ñanderu of Pirakuá Village, in Bela Vista, I was able to reflect on and deepen the concept of the seed in our Kaiowá and Guarani worldview. During our conversations, the Ñanderu revealed that:
  The seed is very important and there are many kinds of it in the forest, it is everywhere. But it does not exist only in the forest, the seed is just like us. I consider myself a seed, I am here because of my father and I consider myself his seed. I am the seed of my father, who no longer exists here in *this world (Ñanderu Jorge Gomes, Pirakuá).*
  79
  Through the Ñanderu’s reflection, I was led to reflect that we are all seeds; our sons and daughters, our grandsons and granddaughters, are our seeds. But not only that — I also thought that teachers, both men and women, who go on multiplying the knowledge of life, are also seeds
  7 Definition from the Oxford Languages dictionary
  multiplying life, and so each person leaves behind their seed, which will germinate and produce life in this world.
  Observing the seeds of plants, one can notice an enormous variety of colors, shapes, and sizes, just as happens with people, who are Black, white, Asian, tall, short, thin, heavy-set. Seeds are the same way — diverse, colorful, with an enormous variety of ways, of shapes, of possibilities of existence.
  Speaking with the Ñanderu, Ñandesy, and elder men and women during this research, it became very clear that we, Kaiowá and Guarani, understand that human beings have spirit, and so do seeds, and that is why the seed strengthens us and makes our existence possible. Thus, seeds have a soul and have an owner, and their strength and spirit are manifested through prayers. When we pray, the owners of the seeds come to bless us; without them we could not live. It is the jara (owners) of the seeds who bring us health and life, from childhood until we grow old, which is why it is so important to cultivate them so that we may have healthy foods, such as mbojape (roasted corn), pamonha, and cassava. These traditional foods, produced from seeds, are what give us health and joy.
  Thus, we Kaiowá and Guarani consider seeds to be a precious gift from Ñanderu. The conversations shared with the participants of this research made me recall the meaning of seeds for our people. I remembered the story told by my ancestors that Ñanderu sent Pa’i Tembeju to walk beneath the earth, and
  80
  wherever he passed, the plant species were born. In this walk of the germination of life, the sacred Avati Morontĩ arose, which carries in the germ of its being the spiritual power to beautify, to perfume, and finally to become food so that we may survive.
  That is why we, Kaiowá and Guarani, consider that all seeds are gifts from Ñandejara, who sent us these beings possessed of a spiritual technology capable of dying and being reborn, generating fruits that satisfy our hunger, feed
  Mother Earth and the other species of nature, besides strengthening us spiritually as an indigenous people.
  Observing the planting rituals during this research, I noticed that for us, seeds, like any other being, require care and attention. Thus, for the Kaiowá and Guarani, caring for the seed is essential, because it is the seed that determines the continuity of life on the planet. Caring for these beings with all love, affection, and respect is what will guarantee the continuity of our lives and the lives of other beings.
  Our people believe that if Jakaira (owner of the white corn) does not allow the spirit of the seed to return to the world of people, then our earthly journey will come to an end. So, in order to prevent this from happening, every year a baptism and planting ceremony is held, carried out by certain elder men and women of our people, who sing and pray throughout all the stages of the seed’s handling and planting.
  Thus, they pray as they clear the soil, as they loosen the earth, and they pray for the rain that must come to nourish Mother Earth. Next, the seed of the Avati Morõntĩ is laid in the lap of Mother Earth, who will nourish it, making it grow healthy in every respect. Throughout its growth, the field is tended and managed through our spiritual technology. Certain guidelines must therefore be followed — for example, women who are
  81
  pregnant or menstruating are advised not to enter the planting area, so that the spirits present there will not wish to enter their womb. Should a pregnant or menstruating woman enter the field, the crop turns yellow and may even die.
  As time passes, and with proper management through Kaiowá and Guarani spiritual technology, the seed is nourished by the whole of this spirituality and develops in a healthy way. When harvest time arrives, further spiritual technological management comes into play, in which the male and female prayer-leaders, chosen people, gather so that the first harvest may be carried out. On this occasion, everyone rises before Pa’i Kwará (the Sun God) and goes to harvest the
  food with great joy and tranquility. They then bring the harvest home, where the women tend to the corn to prepare xixa (a traditional drink) and the men prepare the nhemongarai (baptism).
  In this way, the baptism ritual of this spiritual being, the Avati Morontĩ, begins — that is, the Jerosy Puku and Mbyky, in which the whole people rejoice and lament for the new dawn. In this festival, teaching and the sharing of knowledge occurs from generation to generation; there is no distinction of persons and/or of sex, and everyone, men and women alike, are active participants in the process. And it is in this way that the moments lived and rooted in these spirits make us strong and powerful, both physically and spiritually.
  During my observations and experiences in the planting and harvest rituals, and during my conversations with the elder women and men, I reflected that if even we are seeds, we must consider that these beings are gifts from Ñanderu, for they have the power to reproduce a true miracle, that is, to give life. The techniques used by these beings are of an immeasurable
  82
  magnitude, since, as they are born, grow, ripen, and dry, they go through a process of engagement with the four elements of nature (earth, water, air, and fire), and these elements help them constitute their being through this invisible force that I call spirit.
  Reflecting on the importance of seeds as living beings, I see that the many existing species carry with them this vital energy, which I cannot classify but which I can understand as being our spiritual technology. The whole process these beings go through, from their germination to the stage in which they satisfy our hunger, is a divine, sacred phenomenon that allows us existence and strengthens us as a people.
  When seeds are exposed to smoke for a long time, they often lose their natural color, turning black or grayish. One might then think that the seed no longer has life in it, but in truth it has allowed itself to be painted, smoked, so that within its soul it might be protected from any and all harm
  that might keep it from germinating again. This process of handling the seed so that it can be stored for future plantings is also part of our complex spiritual technology.
  It is this wisdom, this essence, that makes me think and carries me into the ecstasy of reverie when I immerse myself in this context, which for me is more than sacred — it is, in a certain way, supernatural, because in seeking meanings for this natural phenomenon, I encounter the teachings of my people, that everything that exists has a soul, has a jara, and, in particular, the seeds, which are responsible for giving life to all other living beings, making us dependent on this being so small and yet so powerful.
  From this perspective, dialogue with the author Antonio Carlos Sant’Ana Diegues seems quite fitting; he states that biodiversity, for indigenous peoples, is not simply a natural
  83
  resource but a set of living beings that carries symbolic value, integrated into a complex cosmology. According to the author, in the worldview of these populations, humans, spirits, plants, and animals form part of the same world (DIEGUES, 2000). Ñanderu Jorge Gomes’s thinking converges with this perspective when he reflects:
  Our soul is speech, that is, nhẽ’ẽ, and Ñanderu gave this nhẽ’ẽ also to the seeds and plants, and that is why we must pray and sing so that they may be joyful, and sing too, and speak among themselves. The karai are the ones who do not understand what they say, who do not stop to listen to what they say. Father Xa’ĩ is the owner of many plants, and he had chigoe fleas in his foot, so he was cleaning himself and the blood fell to the ground, and that is how the strawberry was born, which is why it is full of little seeds. Wherever the owner of the plants walks, a plant is born. But there is also the plant of the yvaga (sky), the plants of the yvaga sing and bring the seeds down to the earth; in soul and in speech they descend to the earth. It is beautiful to see with our own eyes! (Ñanderu Jorge Gomes, Pirakuá).
  Reflecting more deeply on our spiritual technology, the elder women and men who contributed to this research recalled that in the old days there were none of the farming tools
  that exist today, but Ñanderu would call the frost to dry out the forest, and we would perform the great prayers so as to be able to burn the plot where the planting would take place. According to these accounts, at that time we already had mastery of fire and burned only exactly where we intended to plant. Once the land had been prepared, the traditional Kaiowá and Guarani tool was made for planting the seeds. This tool is made from aroeira or peroba wood and is called sarakwá.
  The reflections built together with the participants in the research also revealed that each seed has its own time to be planted, to sprout, and to grow, in addition to specific handling required for each type of plant. For example, purple-husk corn
  84
  needs five months, taking five days to sprout. With beans and rice, on the other hand, small planting holes are made, and whatever fits between three fingers is placed in them — on average three or four seeds.
  Thus, before the arrival of non-indigenous people, fields were made through the control of fire, and the same held true for dealing with insect attacks and other pests. On such occasions, negotiation took place between the prayer-leaders and the jara of these beings. At that time, nature provided food in abundance for indigenous peoples; there was a diversity of plants that supplied medicines and fruits, a diversity of animals for hunting, and a variety of birds and fish that helped maintain a good diet. In this scenario of such richness, the Kaiowá and Guarani lived in communion with nature, respecting its natural cycles, working the land, and producing a great wealth of food.
  From this perspective, Kaiowá and Guarani prayer-leaders negotiate, through prayer and song, with the jara, the owners of the levels that make up the world, so that, despite the current devastation of indigenous lands, the forest, the medicines, the animals, and the produce of the fields continue to be born. The anthropologist Levi Pereira states that:
  The Kaiowá world is “unnatural”; it does not reproduce naturally, it must be created and constantly re-created through the inoculating action of the
  shaman, awakening in plants, animals, people, and social formation the will to rise up and, in rising up, to affirm its existence (PEREIRA, 2014, p. 228).
  Regarding the action of the shaman, according to the Kaiowá historian Izaque João, “it exists so that the plant may rise up and, in this way, not cause social or personal imbalance” (JOÃO, 2011, p. 29).
  ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
  85
  Thus, our spiritual technology establishes a profound relationship and a constant concern among our elder men and women to maintain our customs, such as the Jerosy Puku and Mbyky, so that during this period the entire community becomes involved in carrying out these rituals, which guarantee the continuity of the seeds — many of them already nearly vanished because of the advance of the colonizers and their infertile minds, as Mr. Jorge Gomes states:
  We were independent, we had seeds of mbakuku, catador beans — there were seeds of every kind, but many disappeared with the arrival of the karaí, white men who came to colonize. And not only us, but also nature, which was and is being exploited throughout its richness. The seeds, in their smallness, hide within their being material the sublime science of remaking life. The spirit of the seed is supreme, it is vital (Ñanderu Jorge, Pirakuá).
  **Avati Morontĩ, the Mburuvixa of the Seeds, and the Jerosy Puku**
  Figure 5. The mburuvixa (leader) of the seeds. Source: Xiru Karaí Archive.
  As we have seen, the seeds are spiritual and divine beings that guarantee the existence of all other beings; however, there is
  86
  one seed that for us, the Kaiowá and Guarani, holds great importance for the balance of all the other seeds: the white corn, Avati Morontĩ. For us, white corn is considered the mburuvixa (leader) of the seeds, since it has skin, flesh, and a heart, where its soul dwells. Without that soul, the seeds are not born, they are dead, and this is why we pray from the preparation of the soil through to the harvest, with prayers, songs, and dances.
  According to the accounts of the female and male elders, Avati Morontĩ (white corn) is the species that possesses the greatest spirit, the one that gives vitality to people's lives. According to Mr. Jairo Barbosa, of the Panambizinho Indigenous Land, a rezador (prayer leader) of that community and of the communities of Gwyra Kamby'i and Laranjeira Nhanderu, this species of corn is Jakaira, the father of the seeds. The rezador tells us that this corn is so sensitive that it must be treated as if it were a child, from the preparation of the soil through to its harvest, when the baptism of the seeds is performed, bringing back the fruits that have germinated.
  The festivities related to white corn and its owner take place once a year, since they must be prepared over a long period of time. Care for the preparation of the soil begins first with spiritual preparation, and only the people chosen at the previous festival may plant the Avati Morontĩ, which is a divinity for the continuity of the Guarani and Kaiowá.
  Thus, once the person responsible for this work has been chosen, the rezador who will keep the prayer of the Avati Morontĩ is invited so that, in the month of August, this rezador may carry out the marking of the area to be planted. This happens in a deeply spiritual way, with the rezador walking and praying in circles and/or in a square from the hour the sun rises until the sun sets. In this way, the chosen area will be sown in September with the seeds that were baptized previously.
  87
  As Mr. Nailton Aquino, puraheita (singer and rezador of kotyhu), tells us, the prayer continues after planting so that the corn will grow, putting out its little ears (bonequinhas) and healthy silk. If this happens, he will know that all is well, that it has been blessed by Ñanderu Guasu, the great God, and that future generations will still come. If everything unfolds this way, Kaiowá and Guarani life and the Kaiowá and Guarani world will continue.
  When the harvest season draws near, a great feast is organized: the Jerosy Puku. The whole community grows euphoric awaiting this great day, and internal and external dialogue begins in search of the food that will be served to the guests. The young people who will do the harvesting before dawn get ready before sunrise, and on this day, while the young people go to the fields, the women go to the prayer house, clean it, fetch the pounding mortar, and prepare everything to receive the corn with much singing and prayer.
  Then, when the corn arrives, people sit down, and between one conversation and another, the work gets done, along with teaching and learning, because the children, the women, the elders, and the people invited to take part in this ritual are all there. The whole day is spent talking, recalling things that were lived, and telling stories
  of courtship, marriages, children, and journeys. While the fire is being prepared, the corn is pounded together with sweet potato, and during this process people dance and rejoice so that the spirit of the corn will fill the space with its scent and its presence.
  Alongside all this festivity, the preparation of the celebration's decorations goes on. The men travel far to gather cedar branches to make the yvyray (path), along which all the
  88
  people invited are led into the great prayer house, where the great Jerosy Puku prayer will take place. It is at this moment that the baptism of the white corn and of all the seeds occurs, along with that of the children and/or adults who have been invited.
  Nowadays this feast lasts three days, so that on the first day prayer continues through the whole night, with brief pauses to drink unfermented xixa. This prayer generally begins at four in the afternoon and only ends around five in the morning, when the rays of the sun travel along the yvyray and reach the rezador, who is there with the seeds, the food to be consumed, and the children.
  There, during this sacred and blessed moment, a great silence falls, and only the faint murmur of the rezador communicating with Pai Kwarahy, the great sun, can be heard very softly. He is one of those responsible for the rebirth of all beings existing in the world, since it is He who is responsible for feeding all the beings that inhabit the Earth with His powerful energy.
  After this moment, the hour of rest arrives, and while the food is being prepared, the children who have already slept and are rested go on repeating the ritual they absorbed during the night for the younger children, who are looked after by the older ones. On this occasion we can observe how a true intergenerational school takes shape in the midst of these sacred moments. This is non-school indigenous education.
  During the day, relatives visit one another, and at nightfall they return so that the feast can continue, such that on this day the kotyhu is sung and the invitation bow for the next harvest is passed from hand to hand. And so the relatives become drawn in, and between songs and
  89
  conversations, they spend the night together in union. In this way, the ritual continues until the third day, when it comes to a close, around ten at night, because by then the xixa is quite fermented. The Jerosy Mbyky is considered the short prayer that closes the harvest cycle.
  Unfortunately, the constant attacks on our people and on our tekoha are having a strongly negative effect on our way of being and living. Nowadays, the feasts and rituals that draw on our spiritual technology are happening less and less frequently, since traditional songs are being replaced by the new generations with electronic sounds, and the participation of the male and female elders is often restricted to the family of whoever is hosting the feast.
  So today, the feasts and rituals still happen, but not the way they used to, when we would stay together for a long time, because now everything depends on FUNAI and on our allies, and we can never gather enough food for many days. Besides that, many of the participants are workers in the private sector and public employees who have set hours to keep.
  So everything has changed; our traditional culture has had to adapt to the context we live in. We have cut everything back, we no longer have time to pray, everyone has to work in different places. Even so, I believe that if we had our roça (garden/field) the way it used to be, with plenty of food, we could also have more days of feasting, of mongarai (baptism), of consecrating the seeds, so as to have more healthy food and health for all our people.
  By growing stronger, we will have greater food production, making possible the return of the animals we used for food and for obtaining medicines, as well as the abundance of certain animal species, such as chickens, ducks, pigs, goats, among
  90
  others. In this way, we will be able once again to hold our festivities such as the Jerosy Puku in their fullness, since we will have food to sustain us through long days of prayers and songs.
  Valdomiro Oswaldo Aquino, political and traditional leader of the Panambizinho Village, said to me during this research, as we were walking through the bush:
  In Paulito's time, everyone prayed a lot. It really was prayer the whole time! Back then there was never a skinny child, no one ever went to the mission, there was no need! Because everyone had Avati Morotĩ food and the children were all baptized (Valdomiro Aquino, Panambizinho).
  On another occasion, in a conversation with Mr. Nelson Concianza, the Keeper of the Crosses, I heard him say: "Now there are no more Kaiowá." For a brief moment I did not understand what he meant. And he went on:
  Every boy nowadays, still a baby, is already messing around with women, no longer has a tembetá8, so who is going to keep the Cross? Here there is the Cross of Paulito, of Ireno, of Lauro, my father. If there is no more Kunumi Pepy, what am I going to do? (Nelson Concianza, Panambizinho).
  I asked him what to do. He told me: "We have to go back to planting Jakaira, before the last ones who know how to pray and perform the boys' ritual are gone. We have to teach, otherwise it will all come to an end."
  And it is precisely against this spiritual weakening that we fight; it is for this continuity of life that we resist. We, the Kaiowá and Guarani Kwery, are concerned not only with our human life, but we are also concerned with the natural balance, we are concerned with spiritual lives, and the seeds give us examples of resistance when they respond to every attack and, uninhibited and exuberant, make use of their spiritual techniques and teach us generosity.
  This sacred resistance makes the seeds come back to life when we provide these beings with spaces for regeneration, but
  91
  for that it is essential to secure the reclaiming and recovery of our territories, so that our seeds may thereby be shielded from the non-spiritual technology of non-indigenous people, who genetically modify the seeds, bringing about their spiritual death. This technology of the whites holds no interest for us, because
  8 Lip ornament worn by Kaiowá men
  it puts an end to the diversity of beings, turns everything into one single thing, and we indigenous people fight for a diverse world, one in harmony.
  ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
  92
  **Tekoha: Our Sacred Land Crying Out for Help**
  Through the accounts of our female and male interlocutors, I was able to grasp how important and sacred the seed is for the
  93
  Kaiowá and Guarani people, especially the seed of the great white corn, Avati Morontĩ. It is this seed that makes the existence of life possible in all its harmony and fullness. But the seed, in order to germinate and give life, needs to be laid to rest in the sacred lap of our great Mother: the Earth.
  During the conversations with the female and male elders taking part in this research, I was able to recall the story of when Ñanderu Guasu set out to create this world, that is, the planet Earth: he went along singing and praying with his kurusu9 in a circle, just as our Ñanderu and the whole Kaiowá and Guarani people do during the Jerosy.
  Thus, wherever he set his foot, land was created, and after having created the land, the Great God went on creating all the things of this planet. Once everything was ready, He created us, the Kaiowá and Guarani, to admire his creation. But today, our Mother Earth is crying out for help; she is tired, she has suffered, she aches, and she is saddened by so much neglect and exploitation of her natural riches.
  The conversations built up over the course of this research made me recall the life of my ancestors, when in the past we all lived, men and women alike, in harmony with our great Mother Earth. She fed us, treated us with care and affection, and gave us everything we needed; but with the invasion of the colonizers, from the sad historical date of 1500 onward, we, the original peoples, were marginalized, exterminated, and robbed. They took our land from us, and in doing so they took from us everything we held most sacred.
  With great sadness and indignation, today I see that the supreme vitality of Mother Earth was, and still is, being brutally plundered by the so-called colonizers, who to my mind are murderers not only of people, but of all living beings and of the
  94
  spiritual beings that
  9 Kaiowá religious instrument.
  inhabit our tekoha. It is a cruelty beyond measure, a disturbing violence, and an assault on life.
  In the course of the research, together with my interlocutors, I recalled that in our region of Dourados, since the 1920s, with the arrival of the Dourados Agricultural Colony (CAND) and the establishment of the Erva Mate Laranjeira extractive company, we were, and still are, being dispossessed and expelled from our original lands. They arrived in the name of progress, in the name of development, but in truth, what they did was to violate our existence as an indigenous people.
  The colonizing invaders confined our ancestors to small areas, called indigenous reservations, and we, unwilling to accept this as our population grew, began the struggle to return to or reacquire our tekoha, our territories of life, which today are in the hands of farmers and large landowners. Only by reclaiming our sacred territory can we live and exist as a strong and healthy people.
  This process has caused immense wear and suffering for my people, so much so that many deaths have already occurred in the midst of this struggle. And it was not only people who were decimated by the colonizers; our entire forest, our cerrado, our wetlands, our animals, everything that has life is threatened by this agribusiness policy of destroying everything in order to plant a single thing. Today, all the species of plants and animals existing in the environment are being replaced by soy and genetically modified corn. That is why our struggle is important: it is for life, it is for diversity, it is for care and love toward Mother Earth and all the beings that exist within her.
  95
  From this perspective, researchers who have worked in Kaiowá and Guarani territory agree that a healthy tekoha is fundamental to the continuity of my people's way of being and existing (BRAND, 1998). Precisely because it is this village, the tekoha, that is the legitimate space for carrying out the rituals, songs, and dances, the liturgies that produce the cosmogony within Guarani and Kaiowá life. It is the necessary space in which to live, plant, and develop (PEREIRA, 1995).
  According to scholars of my people, this space also provides the community with the elements and raw materials needed for the production of typical crafts, traditional food, and the spaces in which indigenous knowledge is passed on. Above this tekoha there would only be the place of immortality, the "land without evil," a space where the human condition is set aside so that the human being may attain the condition of a "God" (PEREIRA, 1995; MELIÀ, 1987).
  The conversations with the female and male elders during this research made clear the importance of a healthy, balanced tekoha for us to be able to live out the fullness of the rituals and to honor the beings left to us by Ñandejara. It is only in this tekoha kwery that we can hold our other feasts, ones without a religious purpose, such as the xixa we make to celebrate birthdays or other commemorative dates, such as Indigenous Peoples' Day, for example. In short: it is only with our tekoha healthy and in balance that we can go on existing in our essence.
  It is because of the immense importance of the tekoha for our people that we fight, day after day, to reconquer our territories, so as not to lose the beings that live alongside us and that give us strength, and also to guarantee the original right of both the peoples and the environment we inhabit. And this struggle needs to be strengthened more and more, because what we see is a constant assault on the legislation currently in force in our
  96
  country, which is being continually threatened by lawmakers who insist on amending it to serve their own selfish, particular interests, causing irreversible harm to populations and to the environment.
  In this way, based on the considerations developed in this research, I can affirm that, for us, good land is the land where our ancestors are, where we can carry out our rituals and sow the seeds within the bosom of our Mother Earth. For us, there is no such thing as bad land; there is sick and mistreated land, wounded and hurt by the many technologies of death that agribusiness cruelly imposes on her.
  For us, well-cared-for land never becomes infertile or sterile; it stops producing only in places where all its energies have already been exhausted through the indiscriminate use of its driving forces, yet it remains humble and lives out the process of resilience with supremacy, patience, and effectiveness.
  The land is capable of reconstituting itself with the help of the spirits that inhabit its depths and its surroundings, and for this reason, we, the Kaiowá and Guarani, believe that as long as we remain steadfast in our pursuit of techniques arising from the spiritual world, we hold the hope of a full life for ourselves, indigenous peoples, and for all the other beings that inhabit this world.
  **Teko Porã: Kaiowá and Guarani Good Living**
  Having thought and reflected together with my people on the importance of the seeds, of the powerful white corn, and of our tekoha for the life and existence of my people, I now present some ideas about our Kaiowá and Guarani way of living, which is based on life lived in an organized and balanced way, through love and respect among all beings. This particular way of life is
  97
  known as good living; for us, the Kaiowá and Guarani, it is known as teko porã.
  Teko porã, in the context of my people, is conceived from harmony with the whole cosmos, with all beings. Our good living means being able to have living seeds, living land, flowers coloring the universe, birds flying joyfully over our tekoha. It means having our children grow up happy and healthy, and our male and female elders living out not merely the utopia of a return to the sacred land, but the assurance that food is for life and not for death.
  Good living, teko porã, is being able to worship the jara kwery (owners of beings) without being judged and condemned as wrongdoers by other religions; it is having time to honor the creation of "God," which today, unfortunately, is damaged, with few species left to admire. It is being able to believe in another possible world, where
  our actions as peoples who care for nature can influence and reverse the course of the history told by the wise lords of a perverse society, one that silently kills thousands of people.
  This is because we, the Guarani and Kaiowá, are not merely part of nature, but are nature itself. We do not think the way non-indigenous people do, who look at nature as an abstract subject, lifeless and without rights. In our understanding, nature is us and we are nature. So when we harm nature, we are harming ourselves.
  Some theorists concerned with the continuity of life devote their research to discussing this theme. These scholars say that, in the context of post-developmentalist discussions, efforts are multiplying toward a reconstruction and overcoming of the conceptual foundation, the practices, the institutions, and the discourses of development. And we, indigenous peoples, are
  98
  showing possible paths by which this reconciliation with nature might become possible, that is, with humanity itself, through involvement (envolvimento) rather than development (desenvolvimento). As the great quilombola intellectual Nêgo Bispo says, we, traditional peoples, do not want development, we want involvement in the building of our relationships.
  According to the intellectual and bem viver researcher *Alberto Acosta, bem viver, or buen vivir:*
  *presents itself as an opportunity to collectively build new ways of life. Buen vivir is not an original invention, nor a novelty of the political processes of* the early twenty-first century in the Andean countries. Nor is it a kind of *superstition or magic potion for all the world's ills. Buen vivir is part of a* great search for alternative ways of life forged in the heat of humanity's struggles for emancipation and for life (ACOSTA, 2016, p. 208).
  In this sense, without downplaying Western contributions, the heterodox views that focus on "alternative developments" must be overcome, when what is increasingly
  necessary is to generate "alternatives of involvement." This is *what buen vivir is about, or bem viver, or indeed teko porã, a* concept developed by indigenous peoples for thinking about life in balance and harmony. We know it is evident that the non-indigenous world is searching for answers on how to live well, but what is needed is willingness and political and social action.
  It is worth highlighting here other humanist contributions, such as that of the Indian ecofeminist Vandana Shiva, whose work has helped spread the debate on bem viver throughout the world. According to this author, the economic and cultural model of the West was conceived through the colonization of women, of native peoples, and of their lands. Shiva thus criticizes modern conceptions of development, economics, progress, and science, drawing attention to the urgent need to
  99
  build a paradigm that makes possible the survival and a dignified coexistence of the peoples and beings of the earth (MIES AND SHIVA, 2007).
  Leonardo Boff, the Brazilian theologian and philosopher, offers the reflection that bem viver points toward an ethic for the community, not merely for the individual. According to this author, bem viver presupposes a holistic, integrative vision of the human being, immersed in the great earthly community that includes, besides the human being, the air, the water, the soil, the mountains, the trees, and the animals. According to him, it means being in deep communion with Pachamama (the Earth), with the energies of the universe, and with the spiritual world (BOFF, 2017).
  Reflecting together with the female and male elders, I found that for us bem viver does not mean living like the karaí. For us, the Kaiowá and Guarani, bem viver, or rather, teko porã, is based on being able to sing, dance, and cultivate the land without concern for large-scale production, but rather in a quantity sufficient to sustain material and spiritual life, both our own (human) life and that of the other beings, in their own material and spiritual lives.
  Because we hold a holistic worldview, we cannot understand how to live without diversity, without spirituality, without care for one's neighbor. In this sense,
  we need to join our efforts and overcome the monocultural model in every respect, and to do so, I believe it is necessary to move beyond the conceptual foundation of development, as well as to change our attitudes and our relationships, because the planet and its inhabitants are crying out for life.
  And to conclude, I say that without seeds, without their spiritual techniques, without our tekoha, and without our
  ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
  100
  Mother Earth, our survival is impossible, just as is the survival of any being, for we form a cycle dependent on one another: we depend on the seeds, on the land, and on spirituality, and these in turn depend on us and on the other species of beings. Thus, if we are not in connection, without this jopoi, we will perish.
  Finally, I close this text with the definition of bem viver, teko porã, together with the critique of the non-indigenous way of life that affects Kaiowá and Guarani bem viver, developed and expressed in the account of Ñanderu Jairo Barbosa:
  Teko porã is eating well, without poison. It is being able to pray, sing, and dance, to hold our Jerosy with good food. It is living without being a slave to work. The white man is a slave to work, and he makes us that way too. Look, our children nowadays don't even play anymore. They go to school, the young person goes to the company and doesn't even learn to pray anymore (Jairo Barbosa, Panambi).
  Figure 6. Jerosy Puku, 2014. Source: Xiru Karaí Archive.
  ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
  101
  102
  **Kaiowá and Guarani School Education and Interculturality: Tensions, Dialogues, and the Strengthening of Traditional Knowledge**
  In this last part, having previously reflected on Kaiowá and Guarani sustainability and spiritual technologies, I proceed to a discussion of these traditional knowledges of my people, from my own point of view as an educator and tireless fighter for a school education specific to my people.
  First, it must be pointed out that perspectives on intercultural education are always in dispute, and today they are being challenged through the struggles of indigenous peoples, aiming at a transformation of the ways in which knowledge is constructed, one grounded in traditional knowledge and respectful of the self-determination of peoples.
  In this sense, this chapter aims to reflect on the specific features of intercultural efforts for indigenous peoples, their tensions, dialogues, and disputes, in order to raise questions and aspects related to this process in school education in the Panambizinho tekoha. At the same time, I have also cast an eye over the experiences of other indigenous peoples built as community educational spaces.
  The proposal is a reflection from the standpoint of a Kaiowá researcher and educator on intercultural processes, a bias of interculturality that has often served as a shallow discourse and as an institutional tool for maintaining the colonizer's policy, since it continues to privilege only one culture, that of the karaí (white/non-indigenous people). I seek to discuss how interculturality can be used as a tool strengthened by communities and built on the ground of the territories. For this, my starting point is the questioning reflection of the
  103
  indigenous researcher Célia Xakriabá: "How do we turn the weapon that colonized us into a space of subversion as well?" (CORREA, 2018, p. 165).
  The diversity of peoples and knowledges is one of the great wonders of the world; this exuberant diversity makes possible the coexistence of cultures and peoples of different ethnic and geographic origins. However, these relations of exchange between distinct cultures generate two-way transformations that may or may not favor the continued existence of the cultures involved, since there is a relation of power imposed by the modern colonial system, which marginalizes peoples who organize themselves socially and territorially in multiple ways. In this way, cultural exchange, known as interculturality, when it occurs between indigenous cultures and Western culture, favors only one side, that is, the side of the whites.
  The ethnocentric and Eurocentric reading of the world has left us a trail of violence, exploitation, and dispossession where intercultural education is concerned. We were led to believe that the only way to build intercultural knowledge is from the knowledge of Western peoples; and this is why I understand that the challenges to be faced in building an Indigenous school education that is both intercultural and just for us are enormous.
  Maintaining the structure of looking at Indigenous peoples as “the others” and positioning itself as a dominant system that masks this marginalization, interculturality has often been called “official” and is sustained by a matrix that subordinates other forms of knowledge and socio-territorial organization; it must be reiterated that this same interculturality was established by the State and by the knowledge of the karaí.
  Top-down interculturality is a monocultural interculturality; it is a denial of multiplicity, seeking a hegemony and a
  104
  coloniality of knowledge and power that is also expressed in schools, universities, and institutes, making Eurocentric knowledge and concepts predominate. The same occurs with
  the perspective of official interculturality, as the author Quijano (1992) affirms.
  Coloniality is related to the pattern of power in the process of domination through a colonization of the imaginary and through the imposition of a paradigm considered universal, as part of European rationality. In light of this, the author Edson Kaiapó (2019) emphasizes that the school, under national ideology, historically created ‘the myth of the generic Indigenous person,’ represented by a set of stereotypes that reproduce structural racism and constant marginalization.
  In this condition, the State creates mechanisms to control diversity through this interculturality grounded in the same structures of power, without even seeking to create possibilities for policies and actions that combat violations and violence against Indigenous cultures. The law of the karaí, that is, the 1988 Federal Constitution, recognized the importance of Brazil's multicultural character, as well as full respect for the original right of Indigenous peoples to their traditional territories, as Daniel Munduruku shows:
  The current Federal Constitution addresses the rights of Indigenous peoples in a transversal, broad, and innovative manner, recognizing that the need for special legal protection for Indigenous peoples lies in cultural diversity and not in civil incapacity, which made possible the drafting, in the years that followed, of abundant infra-constitutional Indigenous legislation, granting these minorities the right to ethnic, linguistic, and cultural diversity, without prejudice to their prerogatives as Brazilian citizens (MUNDURUKU, 2012, p. 37)
  In this context, a series of initiatives began to be adopted for Indigenous School Education, aiming at a differentiated
  105
  education (CAVALCANTE, 2017). However, it is important to note that, most of the time, actions guided by a bureaucratic and institutional vision predominated, through a perspective of interculturality that privileges only the
  interests of the karaí and of the Brazilian State itself, to the detriment of the agendas and demands of Indigenous peoples.
  Thus, although it enables dialogue and a certain notion of tolerance between different peoples and knowledges, this education does not present itself as an interculturality grounded in the valuing of traditional knowledge and spiritual technologies, still less in the sense of an interculturality of a contra-colonial character that is attentive to the struggles of these peoples.
  This process has been gradually questioned in recent decades by curricular proposals in Indigenous schools, as the number of Indigenous women and men teachers has grown, with the orientation of valuing and strengthening the traditions of Native Peoples (KAIAPÓ, 2019).
  The increase in the number of Indigenous educators is fundamental for reflecting on Indigenous protagonism through entry into universities, which for Gersem Baniwa Luciano marks “this new era of the vision and attitude of Indigenous peoples in Brazil” (LUCIANO, 2012, p. 137). The author emphasizes that:
  In the last 30 years, Indigenous peoples in Brazil, in my understanding, made this decision to invest in education. And the very strong arrival at university is part of this wager: school can be an important instrument for the present and the future of these peoples, in every respect, whether for greater interaction with the surrounding world, with the non-Indigenous world as broadly as possible, which shows the great interest in dialogue and coexistence, but there are also specific interests, such as improving living conditions in the villages (LUCIANO, 2012, p. 137)
  106
  Unlike the vision of the karaí and the perspective of institutional bureaucracy, the vision of Indigenous peoples regarding education is multiple and differs in that there exists both traditional Indigenous education and Indigenous school education. Kaiowá and Guarani Indigenous Education, our own system of education,
  always begins in the space of the home, of the domestic fire, in festivals and celebrations, where we learned to do things alongside our elders, learning above all to pray and to relate to the spiritual world. It was always the elders, mothers, and fathers who taught the children and the younger ones. In this collective space of the home we also learned many things about the kokue (cultivated field).
  For us, the Guarani and Kaiowá, especially the elders, we understand the cultivated field not as suffering, but as leisure. It is there that food is born. It is where we can teach our children our way of being. So, the cultivated field is for us leisure and not work (in the sense of punishment that work carries in the Western concept). What differentiates us from this concept of the white man is that the cultivated field, for us, is leisure, is happiness (PERALTA, 2017, p. 4).
  But when it comes to observing the format of Indigenous School Education, one perceives that it is still guided, for the most part, by the ideas and perspectives of the karaí and the State, turning the intercultural proposal into an unequal, unjust, and, worse, colonizing process. From this standpoint, I, as a Kaiowá Indigenous educator and researcher, am quite concerned about this predominance of State interests and the impacts this has on our knowledge, which has already been greatly weakened, violated, and marginalized by the Brazilian State. The school itself wanted to destroy our knowledge. All the knowledge we have kept continues to be violated and may be
  107
  lost if we do not change the tensions and contradictions propagated by the karaí way of being.
  The authors Ramalho and Leite (2020) point out that the establishment and construction of the intercultural school occurred in a way that maintained the exercise of preserving State interests, through a colonizing character and an attempt at whitening that gives little value to the cultures, languages, traditions, and rights of Indigenous peoples over their territories. This process immensely affected our ways of sharing knowledge, where many peoples nearly lost their language, many
  lost their songs, their prayers, and when you lose the language you lose the whole root that surrounds ethnicity.
  In an article written years ago, I pointed to this expropriation of knowledge and the violence of the non-Indigenous way of being toward our people:
  We have watched much of the Indigenous knowledge that prepared the remedies used to cure humanity become the object of a science that ignores our importance in this process of systematizing knowledge. The most absurd thing of all this is seeing that we were expropriated of our knowledge as a result of an inhumane domination that has inflicted upon us a series of restrictions on the living conditions of Indigenous people, stemming from this contact that was, for us, unequal and abusive (Peralta, 2017, p. 5)
  In this context, there are still various difficulties that permeate the school, such as the silencing of the stories told by Indigenous peoples themselves within school curricula, with a colonial view and the mythification and folklorization of native cultures predominating. This is evident both in the fact that we still have non-Indigenous teachers in community schools, and in the marginalization of traditional knowledge, since teaching materials coming from the State end up reproducing the same logic. The lack of strengthening of the protagonism of literature
  108
  and materials by Indigenous researchers in schools is a factor that allows this continuum of marginalization to persist.
  As an educator I am quite concerned about this, about what interculturality seen from a “mono” view can go on causing us, the native peoples. Because it is the elders, the men and women, who ensure that we still have our language and our songs, having managed to guard them with great care and never opening up so that the white man could discover what we know.
  It must be said that when one culture meets another, this could be considered an interculturality, but what kind of interculturality is this? This is the great crux of the question that
  I raise here: Is interculturality my desiring to know the knowledge of the other? The other knowing my knowledge? Because each one has their own knowledge.
  The problem does not lie in sharing our knowledge as different peoples; we have always done this as humanity. However, when this is established from a relationship of a colonizing, hierarchical, and centralizing character, as the State and white culture do, it generates many problems for marginalized groups. The ignorance of the karaí reko (the white man's way of life) institutes in the school an intercultural character that ends up reproducing practices and movements that fully impact the way of being and living of Indigenous peoples.
  But I believe it is possible to destroy this notion of school in this hierarchical format and to think of it instead as a tool through which we can fight for a communal space, in which interculturality is carried out on the basis of our own peoples. I see that few of us, teachers, actually practice this interculturality built from the valuing of traditional knowledge, of our Indigenous science. Perhaps we end up saying we are doing
  109
