  interculturality, but we end up only translating the white man's knowledge.
  In many Indigenous schools there are various events shaped like karaí events, such as the June festival, the graduation ceremony, the Indigenous clothing parade, all in the white man's model. And honestly, I do not know if this is interculturality. White people talk about “interacting,” but when we interact within this white model, the karaí culture is so colonizing that we end up forgetting our own. Now I put this in question: How many of our important traditional events and rituals are held and taught in the Indigenous school? Are we not making room for the marginalization of our traditional ways?
  The intercultural attempts within Kaiowá and Guarani Indigenous School Education, in the format in which they have been carried out and conceived, along a single path where the karaí devise things alone and then
  present the finished project to the Indigenous peoples, is a process understood by our peoples as an inefficient model doomed to failure, besides perpetuating the colonizer's ideal. Therefore, even with some new attempts that have been thought out and theorized, such as, for example, the perspective of critical interculturality as opposed to the functional perspective (CAVALCANTE, 2017), the Kaiowá and Guarani still do not feel fully included when it comes to building fairer and more dignified intercultural knowledge.
  As I have emphasized, these dimensions of interculturality and their historical impacts on our people concern me. I see that this karaí interculturality can bring us a profound betrayal; we give an extra dose of medicine and end up with deep and devastating side effects.
  110
  From this perspective, I agree with the author Gersem Baniwa Luciano (2012), when he stresses that, above all, it is necessary to deconstruct the notions and concepts that inferiorize our peoples and that hierarchize the different kinds of knowledge taught in school, so that it is urgent to undo colonizing ideas, in addition to carrying out a process of “true de-education, that is, learning to recognize the mistakes learned in school itself” (LUCIANO, 2012, p. 141).
  Building another form of education aimed at destroying the colonization of knowledge is fundamental to opening new spaces and political-epistemological axes for rethinking interculturality, from the standpoint of freedom and respect for other cultures, epistemologies, and forms of knowledge construction, as the author Aníbal Quijano (1992) emphasizes. This type of model brought by the white man ends up being imposed on us, Indigenous educators, sometimes without our having any real notion of the effects it may cause and has already caused. So I remain quite concerned, and we need to think much more about what to do with interculturality. I also understand that we Indigenous people do not need to be intercultural about everything, all the time.
  But we are contaminated by things from outside, such that we have already been through destruction, through various kinds of ‘ends,’ and now we are gaining awareness of the effects, even though we have always resisted every process of dispossession of life, of our territories, and of our knowledge. So I remain quite concerned about interculturality, but I also see that if we approach interculturality with respect we can build a more peaceful good way of living, teko porã (the good way of living) and teko vy'a (the way of being happy).
  I agree once again with Gersem Baniwa Luciano (2012), when the author relates that the school institution was
  111
  historically imposed on Indigenous peoples as an integrationist and nationalist project, but was permanently confronted and resignified by our peoples as a tool that enables a less asymmetrical dialogue.
  Thus, in seeking to confront and resignify the school, it is necessary to place our Indigenous knowledge in transit as the central axis for cultivating a differentiated school. This allows the school to gradually be transformed into an instrument for valuing orality, the knowledge of the eldest people, and the valuing of each people's own ways of knowing and doing education based on their own way of being and existing, which in many cases has moved toward valuing Indigenous languages and the oral knowledge of the elders.
  As our relative Baniwa teaches us, only when we strengthen this will a fair and dignified intercultural education be possible, one in which conventional school pedagogies can dialogue symmetrically and coexist with Indigenous pedagogies (LUCIANO, 2012). This is a proposal for a fair and symmetrical dialogue, so that Indigenous knowledge is recognized as scientific, and so that there is an understanding of the educational process as a trajectory that goes beyond the possibilities and limitations of school walls, extending across the whole territory.
  As emphasized by the Indigenous author Célia Xakriabá Correa (2018), many traditional women and men teachers say that the school
  needs to be an interesting place for students, one that should be grounded in the community's knowledge for life, as well as valuing the experiences we live in the territory, where the student needs to understand the inseparability of the body from the territory.
  112
  That is why I also understand that interculturality can bring the possibility of sharing knowledge with respect, since I believe that when I can know and respect the culture of the other, this allows another way of thinking and doing interculturality to be built. As our relative Xakriabá says, “The intercultural experience produces a displacement (or a relocation) of thought” (CORREA, 2018, p. 165). Thus, I can continue being myself, without being the other, without wanting to be the other, and without the other imposing itself on me. From this standpoint, Célia Xakriabá Correa (2018) points out:
  As happens for the most part in academic production, the teaching materials that reach our schools always privilege theories produced at the center. It is as if the culture of the other were stronger; there is a great fading and devaluing of Indigenous students in the academic environment. Some students go to university and are not considered producers, authors, and interlocutors of knowledge in that setting. But there needs to be a reverse process, which is what I call indigenization. Why not indigenize the other? Why not quilombolize, peasant-ize the other? That would be to exercise what is proposed by the very concept of interculturality (CORREA, 2018, p. 19).
  So, interculturality is important, but I think: to what extent is it important for a people who have already endured five hundred and twenty-two years of suffocation and violations? My concern is with not allowing the white man to erase our culture, with not allowing the school to erase our culture. I, as a teacher, have to think a great deal about what I want to do with interculturality. If interculturality is a place of respect, sometimes when we want to respect too much or want to cure a person too quickly, we end up
  giving an extra dose of medicine and it ends up killing. In this sense, interculturality cannot be forced.
  When I think about interculturality, I understand that it is important, a necessary good, but the question is how to build
  113
  this concept collectively within the school. How are we going to build this dialogically and collectively? For there to be interculturality there have to be two cultures, and when they meet, what will happen? They have to dialogue. In this dialogue, to what extent can the other culture have my knowledge? And to what extent can I have knowledge of the other culture?
  If it is not built in a respectful, dialogical, and collective manner, it will continue to be a hierarchical, unequal process with many impacts on Indigenous peoples. From this perspective, the distrust our peoples feel toward interculturality can be understood, since the karaí worldview is not confluent with the native Kaiowá and Guarani cosmoperception; on the contrary, they are opposed. The quilombola intellectual Nêgo Bispo warns that “confluence is the law that governs the relationship of coexistence among the elements of nature and teaches us that not everything that comes together mixes” (SANTOS, 2015, p. 87).
  In this same sense, the Indigenous intellectual of the Kaingang people, in his doctoral thesis, reflects that “the white man thinks of education as the best job, high wages, and understands nature as merchandise” (EMILIANO, 2020). Thus, the limitations of the white intercultural model are questioned by us, the Kaiowá and Guarani. To think of interculturality from the community base and from the valuing of traditional knowledge, it is necessary to say clearly that there is knowledge that we do not want to share with the karaí.
  We do not want to show all our secrets of spiritual technology; this is a memory that the guardians, the elders of my people, both men and women, kept for a whole lifetime so that white people would not usurp it. What we want to share with the karaí are some aspects of mutual learning about
  114
  coexistence with nature, the relationship with the cultivated field and how we build a cultivated field, what the methodology of our people's traditional cultivated field is like, and what it means to be sustainable from our point of view. This we can share so that white people can learn and rethink their way of being and living.
  We can also listen to what the methodology of white people is like in their fields. We can learn what the white man thinks he does right and what may seem wrong to us. This is dialogue; we do not accept imposition. We can discuss how and why white people destroy the land, and also see how they work the land. For example, to recover a territory, let us discuss how the Kaiowá and Guarani reclaim territory and seek to restore the life of the land. Let us think together about how to restore and keep the environment healthy. Let us observe how the white man restores the environment, or whether he only causes damage. Let us reflect on why they use that fertilizer and why we use this one. These are important points for thinking about interculturality.
  Another question relates to a point already raised in the text: so how do we go about this horizontal dialogue? On the premise that not everything can be intercultural. My fear is that our studies may open gaps that further impact our ways of living. Will the school be able to keep our language alive for another five hundred years? Keep our culture alive for another five hundred years? Will the school, through interculturality, manage to do this? So I remain quite concerned, but I believe in fair and respectful dialogue.
  In contrast to intercultural discourses, we, Indigenous peoples, desire an education that is liberating, that emancipates, that is in keeping with our life, our culture, our spirituality, and our histories and trajectories as peoples. It is in this respect that
  115
  dimensions of our political struggle are also inserted. This process involves reflecting on how peoples decide the themes and matters involved in the dynamics of education. Hence the importance of thinking about our own politics, since it presupposes the
  condition for a teaching-learning process appropriate to our sociocultural points of view.
  This differentiated education is a longstanding agenda and demand of the Indigenous Movement, and among the Kaiowá and Guarani it emerges with the Movement of Indigenous Women and Men Teachers (MPGK), as a space of continuous training and political action, premised on the struggle for the right to a different kind of training, one that values traditional knowledge.
  This movement, which operates from within Indigenous school education, has strengthened the emergence of new Indigenous leaders and teachers with a new Kaiowá and Guarani identity, based on the reclaiming of traditional cultural values and the knowledge of other cultures, in a critical and reflective manner, as the Kaiowá researcher Eliel Benites explains:
  These are contexts of deconstruction and reconstruction of values and traditional identities, spaces of continuous training, in which the traditional Kaiowá and Guarani way of being is articulated with new postures, along with the construction of the strategies necessary for political confrontation, with a view to realizing the projects and dreams of Indigenous teachers (BENITES, 2014, p. 18-19).
  Our education is born of the community and prioritizes our own historical, geographical, and sociological processes, our territorial struggles, and our own knowledge. Political self-determination contributes to this end, to our managing our own education ourselves, selecting the kinds of knowledge that should be built and shared in community schools. In this way,
  116
  starting from ourselves, the school and another, possible interculturality can become a reflective space and action grounded in Kaiowá and Guarani values. From this, I want to set down a marker that Indigenous knowledge and sciences are fundamental to another way of thinking about education and to putting an end to the Eurocentric colonization of knowledge, as set out in a text of my own authorship:
  With this, I want to demonstrate that our traditional knowledge is capable of bringing answers to many of the questions that society of today requires, for it is important to understand that we share in this society; we are all on the same road, that is, we are part of the same universe and must care for it (PERALTA, 2017, p. 9)
  For our relative Célia Xakriabá, thinking about interculturality with these meanings allows us to revisit our educational practices, not in a superficial and artificial way, but in an engaged way, experiencing the culture of other subjects, in interaction:
  It is no longer fitting to work with a curricular thinking such as “disciplinarization”; we need, on the contrary, to question this model of uniformization, which makes us always take as our starting point segmentation, in an expectation (which often does not come true) of reaching the whole. In indigenizing educational practices, the proposal is the opposite: the invitation is to start from the whole, from those that are our deep roots, to arrive at the small details, these, thought of always as practices that lead us to act in the world in an active, creative, and subversive way whenever necessary (CORREA, 2018, p. 58).
  And this process can only be built in a horizontal and communitarian way, in which we take ownership of the schools located in our territories, based on our own ways of reclaiming this space. At the same time, it opens up paths that break with the centralism and hierarchy that has always characterized institutional and bureaucratic spaces. From this perspective, the construction of knowledge is a process elaborated on the ground of the village, drawing on the theoretical-methodological
  117
  potential of communities and the praxis of collective subjects who question the colonizing role imposed by institutions.
  In this way, Indigenous thought and its counter-hegemonic practices sow an interculturality that recognizes and values the diversity of epistemologies and the multiplicity of
  worlds and forms of knowledge as an emancipatory instrument of discourse and praxis, as pointed out by the author Jorge Viaña (2009).
  It is a fact that this entire process has been built through great struggle, for we know that in these five hundred and twenty-two years, everything that the Original Peoples have reclaimed and won as original rights came through much resistance, and not because the State was willing to respect the Original Peoples. We know it is a long journey, but we know that a territorialized education is the key to strengthening our peoples and communities, transforming educational spaces.
  As the author Célia Xakriabá teaches us, thinking about a territorialized education means starting from interaction with the territory, and not “merely adding the knowledge produced in the territory into the school, in such a way that this interaction is committed, above all, to the question of the territory, and is operated only from within it” (CORREA, 2018, p. 166).
  **Other Possible Experiences for a Territorialized and Community-Based Education**
  For us, Original Peoples, in the multiplicity of peoples that we are, education needs to be built from within our own communities, in the territories where we live, and with the collective agendas and strategies that strengthen our self-determination and educational autonomy. That is why we
  118
  fight for a differentiated and intercultural education, as discussed earlier, one that truly values horizontal dialogue and our traditional knowledge. It is this movement that allows for the gradual realization of a territorialized education, sustained by the original matrix and by the ancestral struggle to defend our wisdoms, our collectivities, and our ways of thinking/acting in the world.
  In parallel with Indigenous school education, we, the Kaiowá and Guarani, have also built other experiences in our communities, proposing other educational processes aimed at
  strengthening collectivity and traditional knowledge. These spaces are not institutional spaces, but our own spaces, raised up by the community itself, constituting a dynamic of education that is an alternative to the intercultural model implemented by the State. These experiences take up once more the strengthening of our own ways of organizing and propose an interculturality conceived from our own way of being and living.
  These proposals do not present themselves as an immediate solution to all the problems caused by the karaí, but rather are expressed as a path for thinking about new possibilities for the construction of knowledge in community. They are experiences of Indigenous, original education that drive individual and collective emancipation.
  Among our Kaiowá and Guarani people, one of the important experiences takes place in the tekoha Panambizinho, in the sacred space of Xiru Karai, known as an experimental village-school, built since 2010. In this space we combine the management of diverse plants, diversifying and keeping together various cultivated species, in processes grounded in what I call spiritual technology, valuing our knowledge, since the Kaiowá and Guarani are traditionally farmers and have
  119
  always produced rich gardens and fields, which even fed many of the colonizers (PERALTA, 2017).
  The authors Monfort and Gisloti (2020) classify these community experiences as actions built from ancestral knowledge, and from Kaiowá and Guarani practices and knowledge, as spheres of potential for processes of ecological restoration, fundamental to territorial struggles and to new ways of knowing-and-doing education and politics. The energies of Kaiowá and Guarani pedagogy are related to the place where one lives and the place where one is, opening new horizons for thinking about collective paths of emancipation.
  The project still has little support from Indigenous School Education, but it is a fundamental project for Kaiowá
  and Guarani pedagogy, and one that could make a great contribution to the schools located in the villages. Although Xiru Karaí is different from Indigenous School Education, the school institution has much to learn from the autonomous spaces that exist in the community and should value dialogue between these experiences. The school must be open to strengthening the community and the struggle of the people themselves, and not be at the service of a system that has always oppressed the Original Peoples.
  Another experience that emerges among us, Kaiowá and Guarani, is the community space Kurundua, in the Jaguapiru village, one of the villages that make up the Dourados Indigenous Reserve. The Kurundua space, built from the community's political self-determination, was organized by a Ñandesy and a Ñanderu as a community space aimed at strengthening traditional knowledge through sharing between different generations.
  120
  The territorial organization of the Indigenous Reserves imposed a broad process of precarization within an extremely reduced space, contrary to the possibility of living well, of bem viver. Resisting this, one of the principles of this community space is to strengthen collectivity through the Ñanderu and Ñandesy, even amid the difficulties within the Indigenous Reserve.
  Another important experience is the Native Seedling Nursery of the Ñandejara Pólo Municipal Indigenous School, in the Teý’ikuê village, in the municipality of Caarapó, which began its activities in 1997, with the proposal of producing native seedlings for the restoration of springs and forests. The project is linked to the Experimental Unit, which began its activities in 2001 for the management of cultivation practices, animal raising, and the conservation of the region's microwatersheds, based on Kaiowá and Guarani knowledge, with a view to the agroecological and agroforestry system, as demonstrated by Professor Lídio Ramires (2016).
  We believe that restoring our ways of sharing knowledge in order to defend the territory and build new educational experiences stands in opposition to state policy, which aims to maintain the
  order of the karaí and their top-down interculturality. Thus, these experiences spring from Kaiowá and Guarani struggles, in the face of the difficulties of territorialization caused by agribusiness, which constantly tries to colonize our ancestral lands.
  I believe it is possible to think about interculturality on the ground of the community, in such a way that the school engages in dialogue with and learns from other pedagogical experiences and our own spaces, which make possible a community
  121
  education built from traditional knowledge and practices, and which open up other paths for interculturality outside of the asymmetrical interculturality brought by the karaí, in which the interests of the State and the colonizers prevail.
  In this way, thinking about an education centered on theories and practices that are specifically our own is indispensable for the educational process to succeed in Indigenous school institutions and in other educational spaces within the communities. It is this relationship that guides the struggle for an education that is truly ours, in which the pedagogical principle of 'walking while asking questions,' together with the original knowledge and practices of the peoples, wrests control over teaching and learning in Indigenous schools from the hands of the State.
  What I propose to consider here as Intercultural Education is that this construction be grounded in cosmology, in the socio-territorial and ecological relations that arise through traditional knowledge, as well as in respect for our way of life. These are the elements that strengthen the struggle against the monoculture of the mind and that recreate community spaces in defense of life and of territories, seeking the construction of knowledge for life and for bem viver.
  ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
  122
  Interculturality does not necessarily need to involve Western science, that of the karaí, the kind that does not converge with and belittles other forms of knowledge. In this way, I conclude by proposing that interculturality be built and grounded in dialogues with other cultures, beyond the culture white culture
  123
  of the colonizer. May it be grounded in community exchange between our educational spaces and the knowledge of other traditional peoples, such as the quilombola people, the riverine communities, the Pantanal peoples, the fishing communities, in short, the countless peoples of different territories and territorialities. These confluences can bring about another interculturality, different from the one that involves the karaí.
  124
  **Final Reflections**
  In this book, I, Anastácio Peralta of the Kaiowá people, who since my childhood have fought for survival, bring in my own history and in the history of my people the desire for us to be protagonists and sovereign, as we already were in the past, with regard to food, territorial, and spiritual sovereignty.
  In these discussions, I sought to bring forward the question of Kaiowá and Guarani spirituality and sustainability existing in the beings of nature, so that future generations may come to recognize the empirical values in the struggle for land and for our own spirituality, which finds itself weakened.
  More specifically, I sought to focus my efforts on discussing and reflecting on our Kaiowá and Guarani sustainability, which is grounded in our spiritual technology, in the sense of raising ideas and examples that point to paths for sustaining all the beings of planet Earth.
  In dialogue with, and learning from, the elder women and elder men of my people, I concluded that our spirituality and our differentiated relationship with all beings are a type of technology quite different from the technology of white people. Our technology aims at the permanence of life in all its exuberant diversity, while the technology of white people wants to homogenize everything, wants to make what is diverse become a single thing.
  In light of this, I believe that the kokwe (traditional cultivated field) is the model to be developed so that, little by little, we can restore the soil, so as to have an abundant production, free of agrotoxins and respectful of all the beings who live alongside us. In this way, we will be able to achieve our sustainability, a dignified and full life in the Kaiowá and Guarani
  125
  way of living.
  I understand that we are nature itself, and in this way we are capable of responding to all the wounds inflicted on Mother Earth, who
  possesses the power to reconstitute herself, provided that we care for her and give her time to recover. For this, the technology used by the Kaiowá and Guarani people, of making small fields in varied locations, leaving part of the land to rest, can, over the years, resolve soil compaction and degradation.
  The great battle we face is that the karaí want to modify everything in nature, causing irreversible harm to us, since modified seeds and the use of agrotoxins are killing our Mother and all the spirits who live here and who give us life. They even want to modify our culture, our education, our way of existing in the world.
  Nature is at its limit, according to scientists and religious figures of the most diverse beliefs, which is why eco-spirituality is already being considered. This is why the rezadores and rezadoras (prayer leaders) are fundamental, since they use their knowledge and their spiritual technologies for preparing the soil, baptizing the seeds, and planting and harvesting food.
  Thus, by maintaining the sacred rituals of our people, we put into practice what I understand as spiritual technology, understanding that everything is interconnected and in harmony with the cosmos. In this way we are giving the world sustainable answers, leading people to take ownership of their own knowledge and put it into practice. This movement will free us from the great producers of death.
  They stole our lands, destroyed nature, polluted our rivers, stained our ground with the blood of my people. But they were not able to destroy our language, our prayer, our culture, our
  126
  history, our resistance, and our hope.
  And today, inspired by this research, I am involving the tekoha Panambizinho, together with allies who work in defense of Mother Earth, in an agroecological and agroforestry experiment, where the goal is to restore the environment and perpetuate the sacred beings, so that people may have a place where they can nourish the
  spirit and the hope for a better world. Long live the struggle of the Kaiowá and Guarani! Long live Teko Porã!
